segments.en: […I do] not know "ʿAnan," nor "Benjamin," nor any others of this class — for they are dissenters (khawārij) who arose among the nations — I know only "Bayt Hillel" and "Bayt Shammai," who are the root, who were near to prophecy, who took from the prophets and transmitted from them, who are the people of the language (ahl al-lugha), and who are the great number and the multitude. Now if someone says: "This is more fitting to say than [is the position of] one who attaches ʿAnan to the Rabbanites and makes his way in matters of dispute as they do" — [I answer:] this is not permissible. Rather, the obligation is that the religious duties (al-farāʾiḍ) be derived by inquiry and reflection (al-baḥth wa-l-naẓar). Whatever reflection makes obligatory, and inquiry leads to — that is what must be accepted, from whosever statement it may come: be it from the Rabbanites, or from ʿAnan, or from others. Indeed, even if there should appear to the inquiring reflectors a doctrine that no one had ever held at all, its assertion would be obligatory — provided that no objection (ṭaʿn) stands against it and no corruption (fasād) attaches to it.

As for the other class, who are ascribed to being among the Karaites — they are the Persians, such as a group of the Tustarīs and those inclining toward them. For these — despite their parading and claiming of inquiry — censure whoever reflects upon the intelligible (al-maʿqūl), I mean upon any of the "external sciences" (al-ʿulūm al-barrāniyya): whether the dialectical or the philosophical. Two things have barred them from this. The first is sloth in seeking to know the matter, its difficulty for them, and the craving of rest from toil. The second is that some of them imagine that reflection upon the intelligible corrupts the one who occupies himself with it and removes him from the religion — for they have claimed that they saw men who pursued it and whose religion was [thereby] corrupted. This is the source of the suspicion and the slander: for this assertion of theirs makes it appear to the hearer that the intelligible is opposed to religion, shows it a hostile face, and contends against it. But if that were so, then religion itself would lie open to objection — and this is the height of absurdity (ghāyat al-muḥāl). Had they been fair, they were obliged not to condemn the intelligible as the cause of religion's corruption merely because some men reflected upon it and were corrupted; for a [whole] community has reflected upon it whose religion was not corrupted — rather, the matter only increased the strength of their faith. Nor, likewise, was the abandonment of reflection upon it ever the cause of religion's soundness; for a vast multitude has never reflected upon the intelligible nor grasped anything of it, and yet they go forth from the religion and cling to [all] kinds of unbelief (ilḥād). We shall expose the corruption of this assertion of theirs in what follows, and make clear that the intelligible is the foundation (al-aṣl) upon which every assertion rests, and by which all knowledge is brought forth.

I have not seen any of those who lay claim to reflection more faithful to himself than Daniel al-Qūmisī, nor anyone who renders reflection its due and upholds it as it deserves as he does. For everything that reflection disclosed to him, that inquiry led him to, and that the [force of] objection made binding upon him — he adopted and took up. Moreover, he would write to the companions who copied out his books, informing them of whatever had since become clear to him that was contrary to what he had earlier written, and instructing them to note it in his books. Yet he was not stricken with [a taste for] the intelligible; on the contrary, he shuns it, and censures its practitioners in his books at length — though he was strong in Scripture and learned in the language. Even so, a defect clung to him that lowered his standing among our companions: his excess in hatred of the ʿAnanites and his setting himself against them in enmity. At first he used to exalt ʿAnan, mention him often in his books, and call him "the head of the thinkers"; then, from that time on, he took to calling him "the head of the fools." And from one of his stature this is exceedingly unseemly, given the knowledge and the asceticism (al-nusk) that he possessed.

This, too, is one of the great calamities that befall a people from among our companions: their setting themselves one against another and aiming at mutual hatred and enmity. And among the chief things that drive them to it are envy (al-ḥasad) and the craving for leadership (ṭalab al-riʾāsa). It is precisely this [evil] that I have noted which moved me to assemble this book and compose it. In it I intend to revive, in summary form, the statements of the scholars and their arguments — some of it recorded in the books of the ancients, some of it what occurred in the sessions (al-majālis) at which I was present, and some of it what reached me of [sessions] at which I was not. To these I shall add what I have arrived at in the form of question and answer (al-masʾala wa-l-jawāb), and shall discard from them whatever I judged to be corrupt. And where my judgment stood between two evenly balanced [positions] (mutakāfiyan), I have set it down according to their balance — for perhaps another who reflects upon it will see more than has appeared to me. I strive that this book of mine be a mean between prolixity and concision: neither burdensome to the learned nor too subtle for the unlettered. Upon the Creator — exalted be His majesty — and upon all that is good I rely; and from Him I ask what His servant and beloved David, peace be upon him, asked when he said [Ps 119:18–19]: "גַּל־עֵינַי וְאַבִּיטָה נִפְלָאוֹת מִתּוֹרָתֶךָ. גֵּר אָנֹכִי בָאָרֶץ אַל־תַּסְתֵּר מִמֶּנִּי מִצְוֹתֶיךָ." ---

2.title_en: The Enumeration of the Jewish Sects, Each One, and the Age in Which Each Arose

segments.en: The first to bring forth dissension in the religion, to sow transgressions among the House of Israel after the kingship was firmly established, and to alter the religious duties and exchange them, was Jeroboam — for Scripture says of him in more than one place [1 Kgs 14:16; 15:30, and elsewhere]: "אֲשֶׁר חָטָא וַאֲשֶׁר הֶחֱטִיא אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל." This was in his fashioning of the "[calves of] gold," and in his saying to the nation [1 Kgs 12:28]: "רַב לָכֶם מֵעֲלוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִָם." What drove him to this — as Scripture reports — was his seeking to secure the kingship and keep it for himself, and his fear that the people, on going up to Jerusalem, would be drawn to their [rightful] king, who was of the seed of David, so that the kingship would slip from his hand. For Scripture says [1 Kgs 12:26–28]: "וַיֹּאמֶר יָרָבְעָם בְּלִבּוֹ: עַתָּה תָּשׁוּב הַמַּמְלָכָה לְבֵית דָּוִד. אִם יַעֲלֶה הָעָם הַזֶּה לַעֲשׂוֹת זְבָחִים בְּבֵית ה' בִּירוּשָׁלִַם, וְשָׁב לֵב הָעָם הַזֶּה אֶל אֲדֹנֵיהֶם אֶל רְחַבְעָם מֶלֶךְ יְהוּדָה וַהֲרָגֻנִי, וְשָׁבוּ אֶל רְחַבְעָם מֶלֶךְ יְהוּדָה. וַיִּוָּעַץ הַמֶּלֶךְ וַיַּעַשׂ שְׁנֵי עֶגְלֵי זָהָב וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם: רַב לָכֶם מֵעֲלוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַם, הִנֵּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר הֶעֱלוּךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם." A group of our companions has held that he took these two calves only to set them up in the place of the "Cherubim," and this view is not far-fetched — for everything he adopted and dissented in, he meant only as an imitation and a counterfeit of what had been prescribed. The proof of this is his replacing the priests with men from the rest of the nation, for Scripture says [1 Kgs 12:31]: "וַיַּעַשׂ כֹּהֲנִים מִקְצוֹת הָעָם אֲשֶׁר לֹא הָיוּ מִבְּנֵי לֵוִי"; and likewise his appointing the festival in the eighth month in place of the seventh, in the manner of the festival kept in the Temple, for Scripture says [1 Kgs 12:32]: "וַיַּעַשׂ יָרָבְעָם חָג בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁמִינִי בַּחֲמִשָּׁה־עָשָׂר יוֹם לַחֹדֶשׁ כֶּחָג אֲשֶׁר בִּיהוּדָה." It may be that he gave the people to suppose that the year was intercalated, as a group of our companions has said.

This, then, is what Scripture reports that Jeroboam dissented in and exchanged. It may well be that he dissented in many other duties besides, altering and exchanging them, only that Scripture did not mention them, but confined itself to citing the gravest and greatest. For Jeroboam was not one who disbelieved in the Creator — exalted be His mention — nor who denied Him, nor who worshipped an idol, as some imagine. We know this from two directions. The first is what we have already noted: his replacing every duty with another in its place. Had he gone outside the religion altogether, he would have dropped the duty entirely, abolished it, and done away with it, having no need to substitute for it; rather, the cause of his substituting and altering was, as we said, his dread of losing the kingship. The second direction by which we know he had not departed from the religion nor worshipped an idol is this: we see that Jehu utterly destroyed the idols and slew their worshippers in Israel — for Scripture says of him [2 Kgs 10:28]: "וַיַּשְׁמֵד יֵהוּא אֶת הַבַּעַל מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל" — and we then see it reported that he persisted in the sins of Jeroboam, as it says [ibid. 10:29]: "רַק חַטָּאֵי יָרָבְעָם בֶּן נְבָט אֲשֶׁר הֶחֱטִיא אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא סָר יֵהוּא מֵאַחֲרֵיהֶם, עֶגְלֵי הַזָּהָב אֲשֶׁר בֵּית אֵל וַאֲשֶׁר בְּדָן." This is among the clearest proofs that his taking of the calves was not for him as the idolaters' idols are for them. Should someone object: "Has not Scripture reported that he sacrificed to them and offered incense, for it says [1 Kgs 12:32] 'לְזַבֵּחַ לָעֲגָלִים אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה,' and says in another place 'לְהַקְטִיר לָעֲגָלִים אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה'?" — we answer: it is Scripture's way to employ such [language]. Namely, anyone who adopts something hateful to God, in which there is dissent from the religion, Scripture ascribes to him that he has "worshipped it" and "taken it [as a god]." This is like His saying [Deut 4:28]: "וַעֲבַדְתֶּם שָׁם אֱלֹהִים מַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵי אָדָם עֵץ וָאֶבֶן אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִרְאוּן וְלֹא יִשְׁמְעוּן וְלֹא יֹאכְלוּן וְלֹא יְרִיחֻן" — yet the Children of Israel did not worship an idol in the Exile; rather, [Scripture] meant the transgressions that idolaters commit. So too His saying [Lev 18:3]: "כְּמַעֲשֵׂה אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם אֲשֶׁר יְשַׁבְתֶּם בָּהּ לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ, וּכְמַעֲשֵׂה אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי מֵבִיא אֶתְכֶם שָׁמָּה לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ, וּבְחֻקֹּתֵיהֶם לֹא תֵלֵכוּ" — for He then made clear that He meant in this place the forbidden unions. Scripture likewise ascribes to one who pours out his desire upon a particular thing, prefers it, and prizes it, that "he sacrifices to it and offers it incense." This is like His saying [Hab 1:16]: "עַל כֵּן יְזַבֵּחַ לְחֶרְמוֹ וִיקַטֵּר לְמִכְמַרְתּוֹ, כִּי בָהֵמָּה שָׁמֵן חֶלְקוֹ וּמַאֲכָלוֹ בְּרִאָה." For it is absurd that a man should sacrifice and burn incense to the net and the snare with which he hunts; rather, [Scripture] meant the inclining of his heart toward them, that they are the cause of his ease and that by them he made his living broad. So too Jeroboam offered incense in the House of God — exalted be His praise — and set [the calves] over against the Cherubim, and so was said to "sacrifice and offer incense" [to them]; for the Creator had forbidden the taking of [such] images and the offering and incense save in the chosen place. One who dissents in this, taking an image and sacrificing and offering by it and over against it, is as though he had already offered to it. And since the Creator — exalted and sanctified — calls one who sacrificed outside the camp "one who sacrificed to other than God" — as He says [Lev 17:7]: "וְלֹא יִזְבְּחוּ עוֹד אֶת זִבְחֵיהֶם לַשְּׂעִירִם אֲשֶׁר הֵם זֹנִים אַחֲרֵיהֶם" — we know once more that one who sacrificed and offered incense beside an image deserves to have it said of him that he "sacrificed and offered incense to it."

As for His saying "הִנֵּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל," it may be that he meant by it to point toward the Creator and toward the place at which one offers to Him, intending [thereby] the goal of prayer and offering at it. This is like the Children of Israel's saying to Aaron [Exod 32:1]: "קוּם עֲשֵׂה לָנוּ אֱלֹהִים," and their saying when the calf appeared [ibid. 32:4]: "אֵלֶּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל." Did they not say to him, "עֲשֵׂה לָנוּ אֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר יֵלְכוּ לְפָנֵינוּ"? Yet the departure from Egypt had already passed, and the thing they were asking to be made did not yet exist! How could a thing not-yet-existing accomplish what had already happened and gone by? Could such a statement come from anyone not deprived of his reason? What ought to be said in this connection is that the form of the calf is the likeness of one of the faces of the angels, as He says [Ezek 1:10]: "וּפְנֵי שׁוֹר מֵהַשְּׂמֹאול." The Children of Israel, in saying of the calf "אֵלֶּה אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל," meant: this is the form of the angel that brought us out of Egypt — for Scripture says [Exod 14:19]: "וַיִּסַּע מַלְאַךְ הָאֱלֹהִים הַהֹלֵךְ לִפְנֵי מַחֲנֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל." And it may be that Jeroboam meant the same.

From that hour — I mean the hour in which Jeroboam did what he did — dissension welled up among the Children of Israel and those doctrines were sown among them, and they and their successors inherited them one from another. For [Scripture] says of each one of their kings, "וַיֵּלֶךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ יָרָבְעָם וּבְחַטָּאתוֹ אֲשֶׁר הֶחֱטִיא אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל." Nor did they cease from this until the Ten Tribes were exiled. For [Scripture] says, concerning Shalmaneser when he exiled Hoshea son of Elah in the days of Hezekiah and exiled the rest of the tribes [2 Kgs 17:22]: "וַיֵּלְכוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל חַטֹּאות יָרָבְעָם אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה לֹא סָרוּ מִמֶּנָּה." So at the very moment of their being carried into exile they stood upon the sins of Jeroboam — that is, upon the doctrines and the lax rulings that he innovated, exchanged, and dissented in. By now the two calves had already been done away with: for one of them Sennacherib had carried off, as it says [Hos 8:6] "כִּי שְׁבָבִים יִהְיֶה עֵגֶל שֹׁמְרוֹן," and [Hos 10:6] "גַּם אוֹתוֹ לְאַשּׁוּר יוּבָל מִנְחָה לְמֶלֶךְ יָרֵב." So we know that what is said of the Children of Israel at the time of the exile, "וַיֵּלְכוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל חַטֹּאות יָרָבְעָם," refers to the doctrines and lax rulings that he innovated and invented and made into a substitute for the true duties. Thereafter the Children of Judah, too, followed them in that dissension, as it says [2 Kgs 17:19]: "וְגַם יְהוּדָה לֹא שָׁמַר אֶת מִצְוֹת ה' אֱלֹהֵיהֶם," and it says, "וַיֵּלְכוּ בְּחֻקּוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ." They were all exiled while upon those doctrines, were scattered through the world, and have remained upon them, inheriting them down to this day. Now perhaps some who read this chapter will object to its length, since my aim in this bab is only to name the sects, without mentioning the cause of their dissension. Let whoever this befalls know that I did so for a reason that will not escape one who has prolonged his thought upon the matter.

After Jeroboam there arose the Samaritans. They are those whom the nation calls "the Cuthites," of whom Scripture says [2 Kgs 17:24]: "וַיָּבֵא מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר מִבָּבֶל וּמִכּוּתָה…." They are those of whom it is said [Ezra 4:1]: "צָרֵי יְהוּדָה וּבִנְיָמִן" — for [Scripture] reports of them that they approached the heads of the Children of Israel at the time they were building the Second Temple, saying [ibid. 4:2]: "וַיִּגְּשׁוּ אֶל זְרֻבָּבֶל וְאֶל רָאשֵׁי הָאָבוֹת וַיֹּאמְרוּ לָהֶם: נִבְנֶה עִמָּכֶם," and "וְלוֹ אֲנַחְנוּ זֹבְחִים מִימֵי אֵסַר חַדֹּן מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר." It is reported of them that to this day they make mention of "Sanballat the Horonite," who was a chief among them.

After the Samaritans there appeared the heads of this sect — namely the Rabbanites. This was in the time of the Second Temple. The first of them mentioned is "Simeon," whom they call "Simeon the Just." They claim that he was of the remnant of the "Men of the Great Assembly," who, by their claim, were in the age of Ezra and Nehemiah. The heads of the Rabbanites are only [a succession within] a single group, since they followed those doctrines and lax rulings inherited from Jeroboam; for it was they who fixed them, fortified them, argued for them, and wrote down upon them the "Mishnah" and the rest. Among them, one after another, there was at times one who may have brought out the truth in some one duty, yet they united against him and set themselves to oppose him. Such was "Gamaliel," who took the festival according to the sighting of the new moon, and such was "Eliezer son of Hyrcanus," who dissented from them concerning a [matter of] impurity in which they did not [rightly] judge the vessels impure: they decreed against him and separated from him, despite the standing of the wondrous signs attesting the truth of his statement and God's own testimony to it in their account. God forbid that this be in our view as they stated it — rather, they are the ones who report it. We shall later recount the substance of that story as they have told it among the Jews.

After the appearance of the Rabbanites there appeared the Sadducees, whose [founders] were "Zadok" and "Boethus." They were, according to what the Rabbanites have reported, the disciples of "Antigonus," who came after "Simeon the Just," and from "Simeon" they took. "Zadok" is the first who openly opposed the Rabbanites, appeared against them in dissent, and grasped somewhat of the truth. He wrote a book consisting mostly of disparagement of the Rabbanites and invective against them — except that he established nothing of what he said by proof, but stated it by way of mere assertion. Save in one matter: the prohibition of [marrying] the brother's daughter and the sister's daughter, which he upheld by analogy (qiyās) to the paternal aunt and the daughter-in-law. As for "Boethus," he used to say that the Festival of Weeks falls only on the first day [of the week], as the ʿAnanites and a group of the Karaites say.

Thereafter appeared the sect called the "Maghāriyya." They were so named because their books were found in caves. Among them is the "Alexandrian," whose book is famous and well known, the greatest of the books of the Maghāriyya; and after it a small book called Sefer Yadūʿa (?), "a well-known, recognized book," which is likewise a good book. As for the rest of the books of the Maghāriyya, there is in them no book of [real] worth; most of them are tales resembling idle fables.

Thereafter appeared "Jesus," of whom the Rabbanites say that he is "son of Pandera." He is the one known [in Arabic] as ʿĪsā ibn Maryam ("Jesus son of Mary"), and he was in the days of "Joshua son of Peraḥyah." It is said that "Joshua" was the maternal uncle of "Jesus." This was in the age of the Caesar, king of Rome, and in the time of the Second Temple; and the Rabbanites plotted against him until they killed him and crucified him.

It is said that on the Nile of Egypt, some twenty parasangs from al-Fusṭāṭ, there is a people called the "Qurʿiyya." They were so named because they use vessels of gourd (al-qarʿ) alone, to the exclusion of all else. Some of the reporters relate of them that they claim to be the descendants of "Yoḥanan son of Qareaḥ."

Thereafter the Rabbanites split into two sects: "Bayt Hillel" and "Bayt Shammai." The people of Iraq settled upon the doctrine of "Bayt Hillel," and the people of al-Shām settled upon the doctrine of "Bayt Shammai." "Hillel" and "Shammai" took from "Shemaiah" and "Avtalyon." The dispute of "Bayt Hillel" and "Bayt Shammai" was in three [matters], and one party killed a number of the other.

After those whom we have mentioned there appeared "ʿObadiah," known as Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī — [Iṣfahān being a city in Persia] — who laid claim to prophethood for himself. His appearance was in the days of "ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān." It is said that he sought to rebel against the ruling power; men followed him, an army gathered to him, he fought, and was killed. Some of his adherents claim that he was not killed, but that he entered a cleft in the mountain and nothing more was known of him. His [alleged] miracle, by the claim of his adherents, is that he was a tailor and was — as they claimed — an illiterate who could neither write nor read, yet he produced books and scrolls though no one had taught him. In Damascus there is a group of his adherents, known as the "ʿĪsawiyya."

After "Abū ʿĪsā" there was "Yudghan," whom his adherents call "Raʿyā" — that is, the shepherd of the nation. It is said that he was the disciple of "Abū ʿĪsā ʿObadiah," and he too laid claim to prophethood for himself; his adherents claim that he is the Messiah.

After "Yudghan" there was "ʿAnan the Exilarch (Raʾs al-Jālūt)," and this was in the days of "Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr." He is the first to set forth a great body of the truth concerning the religious duties; he was versed in the statements of the Rabbanites, and there was none among them who could fault his knowledge. It is reported of "Hai, head of the academy" that he and his father used to translate ʿAnan's book from Aramaic into Hebrew, and that nothing of his statements passed before them but that they recognized a root for it in the statements of the Rabbanites — except what he said concerning the firstborn, and concerning the distinction between [a child] conceived by a Jew and one conceived by the gentiles; they did not know whence he took this until they found it in the "Ḥazzānūt of Yannai." The Rabbanites strove to kill him, but could not reach him.

After "ʿAnan" there was "Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī," and this was in the days of "al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh." Most of Ismaʿīl's words come down to ignorance, and whoever heard him among the people of solid knowledge would mock him; yet, for all his ignorance, he was inflamed with self-conceit, belittling "ʿAnan" in his books and deriding him much. It is reported of him that he told his adherents, when death came to him, to write upon his grave [2 Kgs 2:12]: "רֶכֶב יִשְׂרָאֵל וּפָרָשָׁיו."

In the days of "Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī" there was also "Benjamin al-Nahāwandī," who was likewise versed in the statements of the Rabbanites and strong in Scripture. It is said that he was God-fearing for many years, and that he succeeded in bringing out much of the truth. Yet in some places he would not make use of analogy (al-qiyās), but kept far from it; and his words indicate that he was bent on following the explicit text (al-naṣṣ), on derivation from the explicit text, or on what issues from analogy with two premises and a conclusion — which is the mean between analogy and the explicit text. We shall treat this chapter further in the Second Maqala.

Together with them and after them was "Mūsā al-Zaʿfarānī," known as "Abū ʿImrān al-Tiflīsī," who was of the people of Baghdad. He was called "al-Tiflīsī" only because he removed to Tiflīs — a city among the cities of Armenia — and settled there; a group followed his doctrine, and they remain there to this day. The adherents of "Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī" claim that "Abū ʿImrān" was Ismaʿīl's disciple and took from him.
After them there was "Mālik al-Ramlī," whose adherents are known to this day as the "Ramliyya"; they are the Malikites.

After "Ismaʿīl," in the city of ʿUkbarā, there was "Mīshawayh al-ʿUkbarī," who was very weak in reflection and was, moreover, like one deranged according to what is reported of him — we shall mention this below. His adherents in ʿUkbarā are to this day called the "Mīshawiyya," and there has never been seen among them a scholar or a man of reflection.
The last who held a doctrine, wrote books, and was followed by men was "Daniel al-Dāmaghānī," known as al-Qūmisī, whose description we have already given in the First Bab.

These are the well-known, famous sects, so far as has reached us. As for the Karaites of this age, who issue from the doctrines we have mentioned, you will scarcely find two of them agreeing on everything: rather, this one dissents from that in one matter, and that one dissents from this in several. We shall later mention something of this. Let us now begin to set out what each sect held as its own. ---

3.title_en: The Doctrines Distinctive to the Rabbanites, in Which All the Jewish Sects Dissent from Them — Save Those Who Followed Them Among the Outsiders — Including Matters in Which They Dissented from the Text of Scripture and Contradicted Their Own Statements

segments.en: We opened by recalling those [sects] only because we have already said that the very duties in which they dissented are the ones inherited from Jeroboam, and that he is the first to bring dissension into the religion. We have already recounted what Scripture reports of what Jeroboam dissented in, and we made it a proof that the nation — at the time it was exiled — stood upon his doctrines, that it was scattered through the world while upon those doctrines, and that it inherits them down to this day; and these are the doctrines of the Rabbanites and their lax rulings.

Let us begin with what they say of the Creator — exalted be His mention. They have permitted concerning Him likeness and corporealization (al-tashbīh wa-l-tajsīm), described Him with the contraries of [proper] descriptions, [held] that He has limbs and a measure, and fixed the measure of each of His limbs — how long it is and how broad. This is found among them in a book they call Shiʿur Qomah ("the Measure of the Stature") — meaning the stature of the Creator, exalted and magnified — besides what they mention of Him in the Talmud and elsewhere of their books, of tales and acts and other matters unfitting even for some of creation, let alone for the Creator, exalted. We shall mention a great deal of this later.

They further claim that this Torah in the nation's hands is not the Torah that Moses — peace be upon him — brought, but is rather what Ezra composed; for the one that Moses brought, they claim, was lost, fell away, and vanished. This is to bring down the religion utterly. Had the Muslims taken up this statement of the Rabbanites, it would have been a great proof in their hands and an argument for them; for some of their controversialists already argue against us, saying that the Torah you possess is not the Torah Moses brought — and we conclude against whoever among them argued this that he has lied and contradicted himself, and that what drove him to it was vainglory and the laying of an objection against us. But had they grounded it on the Rabbanites' own statement, they would have had a broad answer and would have needed nothing else.

Of this also: that they discarded prayer from the "Book of Psalms" and made it instead from what they themselves composed. This contradicts what Scripture reports, for it says [Ezra 3:10]: "לְהַלֵּל אֶת ה' עַל יְדֵי דָּוִיד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל." And yet they say at the head of their prayer: "אֲשֶׁר בָּחַר בְּעַבְדּוֹ דָוִד וְרָצָה בְּשִׁירוֹתָיו…," and the rest of the formula. So they have admitted by this saying that praise and laud of God — exalted be His praise — is an obligation from David's words. Yet they did not take it up as it ought to be taken; rather they say it while seated, merely by way of recitation and mention. We shall complete the matter with proof in its place.

They forbade people to press their faces to the ground when prostrating. This contradicts the saying of Scripture [2 Chr 7:3]: "וַיִּכְרְעוּ אַפַּיִם אַרְצָה עַל הָרִצְפָה וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ." Moreover, at the end of the prayer they do what the Christians do, bowing right and left, claiming that this bow is to the two angels appointed over each person, one on a man's right and the other on his left. More astonishing still: they begin with the bow toward [the angels], and only afterward bow to the Creator — magnified and glorified — which is the bow toward the front.

With this, they ask the angels to convey their prayers to the Creator — exalted and exalted — that they may make Him hear their supplications and [pleas for] mercy. This is in their saying: "מַכְנִיסֵי רַחֲמִים, הַכְנִיסוּ רַחֲמֵינוּ לִפְנֵי בַּעַל הָרַחֲמִים." They have interpreted in this sense the saying of Solomon [Eccl 10:20]: "אַל תְּקַלֵּל מֶלֶךְ בְּמַדָּעֲךָ" — claiming he meant by it the Creator, magnified and glorified — and his saying [ibid.]: "וּבַעַל הַכְּנָפַיִם יַגֵּיד דָּבָר" they referred to the mention of the angels, of whom it is said [Isa 6:2]: "שֵׁשׁ כְּנָפַיִם שֵׁשׁ כְּנָפַיִם לְאֶחָד." So they claim that Scripture reports thereby concerning the Creator — far exalted is He above this! He it is who described Himself in saying [Jer 32:27]: "הִנֵּה אֲנִי ה' אֱלֹהֵי כָּל בָּשָׂר, הֲמִמֶּנִּי יִפָּלֵא כָּל דָּבָר?" and says [ibid. 32:17]: "לֹא יִפָּלֵא מִמְּךָ כָּל דָּבָר"; and of whom it is said [Dan 2:22]: "הוּא גָּלֵא עַמִּיקָתָא וּמְסַתְּרָתָא, יָדַע מָה בַחֲשׁוֹכָא." Does One whose description is this stand in need that a statement or speech reach Him or be conveyed to Him?

Of this: they permitted on the Sabbath that a man ask of his fellow a jar of wine and a jar of oil; this is in their saying [M. Shabbat 23:1]: "שׁוֹאֵל אָדָם מֵחֲבֵרוֹ כַּדֵּי יַיִן וְכַדֵּי שֶׁמֶן, וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמַר לוֹ הַלְוֵנִי, וְכֵן הָאִשָּׁה מֵחֲבֶרְתָּהּ כִּכָּרוֹת. וְאִם אֵינוֹ מַאֲמִינוֹ, מַנִּיחַ טַלִּיתוֹ אֶצְלוֹ, וְעוֹשֶׂה עִמּוֹ חֶשְׁבּוֹן לְאַחַר הַשַּׁבָּת." This is buying and selling on the Sabbath in fact — only that it is a stratagem (ḥīla), as he said [Jer 9:4]: "הַעֲוֵה נִלְאוּ." And concerning the "ʿeruv ḥaṣerot" they said what is famous and known to everyone.

They permitted a man to write on the Sabbath one letter or two, provided it is not a complete name or a single [whole] word. As though, had he written "dalet–nun" intending the name "Dan," he would be a sinner, since it is a complete name; but had he written "dalet–nun" intending part of the letters of "Daniel," he would not be a sinner, since he did not write a complete name. Likewise they permitted a weaver to weave into a garment one thread or two from which no folded [piece] results — that is, a portion of a garment.

They permitted intercourse on the day of the Sabbath, in which there are three things contrary to what we were commanded concerning the Sabbath: the first — motion and exertion, contrary to [Exod 20:10]: "לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה כָל מְלָאכָה"; the second — the contracting of impurity, contrary to the sanctity that is obligatory on the Sabbath; the third — the emission of seed, contrary also to His saying [Exod 34:21]: "בֶּחָרִישׁ וּבַקָּצִיר תִּשְׁבֹּת."

They permitted these things whose contrary is manifest, and forbade things whose very opposite the senses attest. Of this: that a man should not prostrate on the day of the Sabbath — lest he ask of his Lord a need, there being no prayer that they or others pray that does not contain the asking of needs. How is it permitted that a man ask his Lord a need standing or seated, and not permitted that he ask while prostrate? And how is it permitted that he say in his prayer: "תּוֹלֶה רַחֲמֶיךָ וְתָאֶת כַּעַסְךָ, וְהַצִּילֵנוּ וְכָל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִדֶּבֶר וַעֲוֹנוֹת" — which is the asking of needs for himself and for all the House of Israel — yet not permitted that he ask a need for himself alone?

More astonishing than this — that they claim in the "halakha" that what the gentiles have sown and planted becomes pure by their drawing near to it; for they did it in the name of idolatry, and Scripture has said [Isa 30:22]: "וְתִזְרֵם כְּמוֹ דָוָה" — which requires that eating it be forbidden, and that the Children of Israel, on entering the land of al-Shām, ate neither of its crops nor of its fruits. With what heart do they bear this?

They likewise forbade a man to bring his hand to his mouth (to eat) while walking less than four cubits — yet one does not know the ruling on urine and excrement! Is there in [all] doctrines anything more frivolous than this doctrine?

It is a wonder that they forbade a man to put straw in a sieve on the day of the Sabbath — lest a speck of straw fall through the sieve, so that he would be as one who sifted on the Sabbath — yet permitted one whose roof-beam broke on the Sabbath to bring a board and place it under that beam to prop it up. Is there a stronger self-contradiction than this — that they forbade what is unintended, and permitted the [very] intention itself?
They also permitted a man to cook on the Sabbath — by preparing the pot before the Sabbath and setting it in the oven — so that it cooks on the Sabbath and is eaten on the Sabbath.
Of this: they made obligatory the circumcision of a dead [infant], which reason rejects in the utmost.

Of this: they abolished impurity for all people in the Exile. This is in their saying: "מִשֶּׁחָרַב הַבַּיִת, לֹא טוּמְאָה וְלֹא טָהֳרָה." They claimed there is none impure from leprosy nor pure from [contact with] the dead, and by this saying brought down all the [laws of] impurity. For with them — if the corpse, which is the gravest of impurities, yields no purification, then all people in this age are impure, and they are not on guard concerning what they have touched or contacted of the other impurities. For if the grave impurity has befallen them, and they have no cleansing or purification from it, then what is below it already envelops them; yet they pray, touch the scrolls and the "holy [writings]," and this for them is impermissible. In this connection they spoke words that contradict this saying: they claimed that they permitted the impure to touch the scrolls — because the scrolls are written on impure hides, being from the beasts of the gentiles. We say to them: why did you permit scrolls to be written on the hides of gentiles — when in this permission you have joined impurity and purity? They claimed they did so in order that scrolls might be plentiful in people's hands, and that had they permitted scrolls to be written only on Jewish hides, scarcely a scroll or sheet of the Torah would be found, and reading would dwindle in the nation. Do you not see the clear flaw in this? — for we know that in a single city there is already found, of the hides that Jews slaughter, what would suffice for all the scrolls and books of the world! We also said to them: is it not possible that among the scrolls are some whose hides are from a Jew's beasts? Why have you mixed everything into a single rank?

They further contradicted what they made obligatory concerning the abolition of corpse-impurity in this age — that there is no purification from it — from another angle: that they forbid the priests to draw near to the dead or to carry corpses to the graves. For if there is no impurity and no purity, but all people are impure, and they pray and read the books and scrolls nonetheless, the impurity that befell them not preventing them — what is this special status by which the priests must be singled out for this prohibition? If they excuse themselves by the saying of Scripture [Lev 21:2]: "כִּי אִם לִשְׁאֵרוֹ הַקָּרֹב אֵלָיו" — the answer is that this dispensation took effect only when there was something by which purification could be had; so why have you permitted it now, when purification is not to be found?

More astonishing than this — that the corpse of one of the gentiles, with them, does not convey impurity. This contradicts what Scripture reports, that the Children of Israel were commanded to become impure from the people of Midian, in His saying [Num 31:19]: "וְאַתֶּם חֲנוּ מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה שִׁבְעַת יָמִים." They excused this claim by saying that Scripture said [Num 19:14]: "אָדָם כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל"; they said: "adam [man] means only Israel," per His saying [Ezek 34:31]: "וְאַתֵּן צֹאנִי, צֹאן מַרְעִיתִי, אָדָם אַתֶּם." They further claimed that one who touched a corpse's bone — if it is broken — does not become impure, per His saying [Num 19:16]: "אוֹ בְעֶצֶם אָדָם" — woe to whoever said this! Did he not know that the part of a bone is bone, even if it is a fragment of it, just as the finger is a part of flesh and is flesh?

They said [M. Niddah]: "מֻתֶּרֶת הָאִשָּׁה הַנִּדָּה לְשַׁמֵּשׁ בְּכָל צָרְכֵי הַבַּיִת," and said in the Talmud [Ketubbot 4b]: "כָּל מְלָאכוֹת שֶׁהָאִשָּׁה עוֹשָׂה לְבַעְלָהּ, נִדָּה עוֹשָׂה לְבַעְלָהּ" — meaning that all a wife may do for her husband, a menstruant may do: cooking, baking, handling clothes and vessels, and the rest. Yet they specified three things they did not permit her: that she not spread his bed, not light his lamp, and not mix his cup. So they permit her to cook and bake for him what he eats, but do not permit her to light the lamp — in which there is neither harm nor benefit nor impurity clinging to a person. And concerning the "seven days of purity" they said what God did not command.

Graver than this is your saying that only the priest recognizes a [genital] flux (zivah), and that the woman — if she saw the blood — would convey it to him until he should tell her whether it is menstrual blood or flux-blood. They relied on the saying of Scripture [Deut 17:8]: "בֵּין דָּם לְדָם," which no one possessed of sense — let alone of full reason — would doubt was meant only as a distinction between healthy blood and diseased blood. They claimed that the one with a flux is not reckoned a full flux-sufferer until he sees the flux three times — which God did not say.

Of this: that if the impure is mixed with sixty times its measure of the pure, the pure does not become impure from that impurity and is not forbidden. With them — if a dead mouse or pork fell into wine or vinegar of sixty times its measure, and then was crushed and dispersed, eating and drinking the thing it fell into is not forbidden. By this saying they eat the impure outright. Likewise they permitted the worm that breeds in fruit, flesh, fish, and beans, and all the like — this being as the first, or graver. They permitted the fat-tail (alyah) explicitly forbidden among the [forbidden] fats, and likewise the kidneys and the lobe of the liver.

Of this: their permitting of the "ben pequʿa," and their saying that even had it plowed a field for five years, the slaughter of its mother would render it pure. With them — had a ewe or cow been slaughtered when the time of its bearing had come, and its belly then cut open and a young one come forth that lived five years — that young one needs no slaughter for whoever wishes to eat it, and nothing of it is forbidden at all. By this saying they have permitted seven of the forbidden things: first — carrion; second — blood; third — fat; fourth — a limb from the living; fifth — "it and its young"; sixth — the slaughter of a non-Jew; seventh — the sciatic nerve. And it follows for them by this saying that if a ewe or cow died at the time of its bearing before it gave birth, and its belly was then cut open and the young came forth alive and then lived as long as it lived — its eating would never be permitted; for it is part of the dead, and what was part of the dead may not be eaten. For if its mother's slaughter purified it and permitted it, this requires that its mother's death rendered it impure and forbade it.

They permitted all this, and forbade what God did not forbid and for which no root is found — namely what they claimed of the "ṭerefot" discernible by inspecting the lung, and what they mentioned of the conditions of slaughter in the "law of slaughter" (sharīʿat al-shaḥṭ), which are: pausing (shehiyah), pressing (derasah), burrowing (ḥaladah, of the knife), tearing (hagramah, the knife's deviation), and slaughter with a notched knife. In all these they dissented from the saying [Deut 13:1]: "לֹא תֹסֵף עָלָיו וְלֹא תִגְרַע מִמֶּנּוּ."

Among the wonders — what they made obligatory of restricting the [amount of] flesh, which the reports of Scripture refute, for they [show] the multitude of offerings on [festal] occasions, such as His saying [1 Kgs 3:4]: "וְהֶעֱלָה שְׁלֹמֹה אֶלֶף עֹלוֹת," and like the Passover and the rest. Would any sensible person accept that all this had someone to consume it, or that there was at any time what could bear it? Does any doubter doubt that most of these things were done only by way of a symbolic act?

More wondrous still — that they forbade putting the meat in the pot in cold water except after the water has boiled; for they claimed that if meat is put into cold water and then the whole is boiled, the blood dissolves into the water and is consumed; but if the water is boiled and the meat then put in, it does not dissolve into it. From this saying of theirs it follows that eating the blood within the very flesh is permitted, but in the broth forbidden. The like seals upon them in their forbidding the cooking of the liver and the spleen — for they permit eating them roasted. Similar is that they permit roasting the fish whole and cooking it with its blood and eating it; but if the blood came out of it without disturbance, its blood is forbidden to eat. They permitted eating the floating dead fish, explicitly [declared] carrion — to the point that they claimed that if a dead, impure fish was caught and a pure fish found in its belly, eating the pure one is permitted. This they permitted, and forbade meat with milk.

They claimed that the bones of carrion and of a ṭerefah, and their hide, are not forbidden to eat; rather, only eating the flesh is forbidden, per His saying [Exod 22:30]: "וּבָשָׂר בַּשָּׂדֶה טְרֵפָה לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ." It then follows for them that they should permit eating the bones and hide of swine, if Scripture forbade only eating its flesh. Likewise it follows concerning the fat, the liver, the spleen, the lung, and the marrow — that none of these is forbidden, since none of them is flesh, and only eating the flesh was forbidden. And if it were obligatory that all these be forbidden by analogy to the flesh, then eating the hide and bone would be forbidden too, by analogy to the flesh.

They admitted that the heads of the months used to be fixed by sighting the moon, and dissented from this by fixing them through the intercalation of the month (ʿibbur) built on the rule "not on [days] 2, 4, 6," for which no obligating cause is known; it is what "Isaac son of Bakhī" did. Hai, head of the academy, already mentioned this in a book he composed, as did [other] people, concerning the intercalation of the month. The rule "not on 2, 4, 6" has two [explanations]: some claim they did it so that the seventh day of the Festival of Booths should not fall on the Sabbath — for [otherwise] the gifts and offerings would be withdrawn, since it was the practice of those who attended the Temple to give the gifts on the seventh day of the Festival of Booths, and if it fell on the Sabbath, there would be a defect and disruption in this. Others claim they did it so that the Day of Atonement should not fall on a Friday or a Sunday; for if a death occurred on Friday — which was the Day of Atonement — and a Sabbath preceded it, or a death on the Sabbath followed by the Day of Atonement, the corpse would remain two days and two nights and putrefy.

They claimed that [Num 33:3] "מִמָּחֳרַת הַפֶּסַח," on which the Children of Israel went out of Egypt, was the sixteenth of Nisan — contrary to the text's saying [ibid.]: "וַיִּסְעוּ מֵרַעְמְסֵס בַּחֹדֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן," and His saying [ibid.]: "מִמָּחֳרַת הַפֶּסַח יָצְאוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל" on the fifteenth day of the month. Likewise they claimed that what remained of the Passover was burned on the sixteenth of Nisan, contrary to His saying [Exod 12:10]: "וְהַנֹּתָר מִמֶּנּוּ עַד בֹּקֶר בָּאֵשׁ תִּשְׂרֹפוּ."

Of their self-contradictions: they claimed that one who has an uncircumcised person in his house may not eat the Passover. Yet they claim that the Children of Israel used to slaughter the Passover for forty years in the wilderness, and among them was a group of the uncircumcised — namely those born in the wilderness, per His saying [Josh 5:7]: "כִּי עֲרֵלִים הָיוּ, כִּי לֹא מָלוּ אוֹתָם בַּדָּרֶךְ."

They permitted leaven to be brought into a Jew's house during the seven days of unleavened bread, if it is not his own — by there being in his house a man not of the religion's people, for whom, as an "outsider," it is permitted to bring leaven into the Jew's house. They excused themselves by His saying [Exod 13:7]: "לֹא יֵרָאֶה לְךָ חָמֵץ"; they said: this forbids it to you, but to another than you it is not forbidden. In this sense there are two kinds of corruption: the first, that it contradicts the text, for He says [ibid. 12:19]: "לֹא יִמָּצֵא בְּבָתֵּיכֶם"; the second, that in this they contradict themselves, for they forbade our having leaven in another's house alongside Scripture's saying "בְּבָתֵּיכֶם." For if by His saying "לְךָ" He forbids only to you and not to another, then by His saying "בְּבָתֵּיכֶם" He forbids only what is in our houses and not in the houses of others.

They made obligatory the seeking of the new barley (aviv) and the taking of the Passover upon it — and contradicted this by their saying concerning the intercalation of the month. I shall recount some of what is in their books that brings the matter down, and this is in the Seventh Maqala, in which the heads of the months and the new barley are treated.

Among what they dissented in against the text plainly: Scripture made obligatory concerning the "goring ox" that if it killed a person, its owner is put to death, per [Exod 21:29]: "וְהַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל וְגַם בְּעָלָיו יוּמָת" — yet they claimed he is not put to death.

They discarded the standing [daily] prayer (the morning tamid) on the Day of Atonement, for whose obligation there is no support; for they open with the afternoon prayer of the Day of Atonement and follow it with the "additional" (musaf). They made obligatory a prayer that is not known — the one they call the prayer of "neʿilah," which they pray at the end of the day.

They claimed that the time of the aṣīl is from midday to sunset, and then contradicted this by saying in the "Mishnah" [Negaʿim 2:2] that the leper is not inspected at dawn, nor at midday, nor at the two declines [of the sun], but is inspected in the seventh hour, the eighth, and the ninth. This indicates that those three hours are not of the time of the aṣīl that they claimed to be from midday to sunset.

They did not make obligatory — if two or three "additional" [prayers] fall on a single day, such as the New Year falling on a Sabbath, where three "additionals" would be obligatory: the additional of the Sabbath, of the New Moon, and of the New Year — they did not make obligatory of the three more than a single prayer in which the three matters are mentioned. And if this is permitted, it would have been permitted that these be mentioned in the standing [daily] prayer, with no need for another prayer. So they contradicted the obligatory prayers, and made obligatory an added prayer they called the prayer of [the afternoon].

Scripture said [Lev 23:40]: "וּלְקַחְתֶּם לָכֶם בַּיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן" — commanding the taking of [certain] things for making the booth, as was interpreted and explained in Ezra [Neh 8:15]; yet they claimed it is only for the willow branch, and that the "taking" is only a taking in the hand. Scripture made obligatory the keeping of the festival-day one day in each festival — they made it two days. Likewise it made obligatory the eating of unleavened bread seven days, and dwelling in the booth seven days — they made them eight.

Of this, their saying: that one who died childless, his inheritance went to his brother, who would do the levirate to his wife, and to none else. Likewise, that one who died leaving a young daughter together with a son, [the daughter] must take a tenth of the inheritance; but if she was of age, she must take nothing at all of her father's property, and is left to die of hunger. What cause is it that distinguished between the minor and the adult [daughter] in inheritance? Is this ruling not in the category of [Hab 1:4]: "יֵצֵא מִשְׁפָּט מְעֻקָּל"?

As for the people of al-Shām — they made obligatory examination by the finger (before intercourse), and whoever submitted to the argument for it claimed that it is obligatory only so that a man not proceed to engage in something forbidden; for he does not know whether the woman he wishes to lie with is sound and clean, or has already engaged in something forbidden and corrupt. If she did so and he then came to her, he would have come upon something forbidden; but if he examined her with the finger, he would be safe from engaging in the forbidden. We say to the holder of this saying: if this is obligatory, then by its [logic] it follows that a man is obliged — every time he wishes to come to his wife — to test her with the "water of the suspected adulteress" (mei sotah); for he is not secure that she has not already engaged in corruption! So that — if he came to her without testing — he would have come upon the forbidden; and the whole House of Israel would then need to lock up their wives every single day until they bring them to the Temple, and only then engage with them, and to separate from them their nights and days! Rather, what we have said is more fitting and more binding than what they said and made obligatory: namely, that he who wishes to lie [with her] should ascertain the woman's soundness or corruption from the moment he begins with her, before the completion of the act — and then, if he saw the matter to be improper, he could properly abstain from the act.

They said of the unmarried woman — who is the unattached one: if she was alone with [several] men, some of whom are permitted to marry her and some not — that is, her [forbidden] kin — and one of them came to her and she bore a child: if she said the child is from the forbidden kin, the child is a "mamzer"; but if she said it is from those permitted to marry her, the child is legitimate. We say to them: glory be to God! Is it permitted that her statement and testimony be accepted, when she herself is a fornicatress?

They claimed that if a man's wife bore a child: if that child was from a non-Jew or a Jewish slave — whether she was compelled by one of them or [willingly] submitted — the child is legitimate. They made the Jewish slave like a non-Jew, [yet] he is subject to the commandments, and obligatory upon him is [Lev 20:10]: "מוֹת יוּמַת הַנֹּאֵף וְהַנֹּאָפֶת" — his ruling is the ruling of the native-born.
They said that one who raped a woman and lay with her may marry her daughter, contrary to [Lev 18:17]: "עֶרְוַת אִשָּׁה וּבִתָּהּ לֹא תְגַלֵּה."

[The text here is partly corrupt.] They permitted marrying the half-sister from a foreign mother or from another [father]; and an analogy follows for them in this, since the divorced woman, if she fornicated, may not return to her husband, per His saying [Jer 3:1]: "וְאַתְּ זָנִית רֵעִים רַבִּים, וְשׁוֹב אֵלַי, נְאֻם ה'." [They named some fifteen women freed by the death [of a relative] and by the loosing of the sandal — the daughter, the son's daughter, the daughter's daughter, and the rest of the [forbidden] kin — yet permitted others by analogies that contradict the very prohibitions.]

They said concerning [Jer 17:22]: "וְלֹא תוֹצִיאוּ מַשָּׂא מִבָּתֵּיכֶם" — that carrying out and bringing in on the Sabbath is forbidden. Then they said: one who carried from one domain to another is not a sinner unless his hand carried a thing from one place to another place and set it down in another place. But if his hand was outstretched and a man placed a purse in it, and he drew his hand from domain to domain, he is not a sinner. Then they explained this in the "Mishnah" [Shabbat 1:1]: "יְצִיאוֹת הַשַּׁבָּת שְׁתַּיִם שֶׁהֵן אַרְבַּע."

They said concerning [Exod 21:15]: "וּמַכֵּה אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ" — that he is not a sinner unless he strikes them both together; but if he struck them separately, he is not [liable]. So too with cursing. And they said of [Deut 21:18] "בֵּן סוֹרֵר וּמוֹרֶה" — that there never was and never will be [such a case]. This shows that whoever founded this saying is either trifling or a fool.

They said: one who vowed a vow and regretted it goes to a sage to absolve him of his vow, per their saying [Ḥagigah 10b]: "הוּא אֵינוֹ מַתִּיר אֶת נִדְרוֹ, אֲבָל אֲחֵרִים מַתִּירִין." They said in the "Halakhot Gedolot": one who has a vow or oath upon him and wishes to be released — goes to the Rabbanites that they absolve him, if the one who vowed says, "I did not swear with [such-and-such] intent," and then they absolve him for it. Of them is the saying [Ps 89:35]: "וּבְרִיתִי לֹא אֲחַלֵּל" — and is this permitted to another than Him? Did He not say [Zech 5:4]: "הוֹצֵאתִיהָ, נְאֻם ה' צְבָאוֹת"?

They claimed that one who consummated [a marriage] may not return to intercourse except after seven days — lest menstrual blood come out with the blood of the [broken] hymen, so that he would have come upon a menstruant. We say to them in this: if this is obligatory, then it follows that he becomes impure every time he draws near her during those seven days — for he is not secure that she is not a menstruant.

Of this — their permitting the brother's daughter and the sister's daughter, between whom and the paternal aunt and daughter-in-law there is no difference; for reason does not distinguish between the [paternal] uncle and aunt and the maternal uncle and aunt.

What is more astonishing than that one blesses over the lamp of the Sabbath eve, claiming in his blessing that God commanded it? Likewise the lamp of the festival of Ḥanukkah. More astonishing still — their saying concerning the compounding of the incense. That is: the incense which Scripture reported to be of four things [Exod 30:34], "נָטָף וּשְׁחֵלֶת וְחֶלְבְּנָה, סַמִּים וּלְבֹנָה זַכָּה" — they added [more] things, namely: balsam, musk, sandalwood, and floating-storax. Likewise, Scripture reported that they should be equal parts — yet they made some of them seven, some nine, and some three.

They have, in the laws of marriage, manifestly ugly and corrupt matters whose exposition would be lengthy. I have left off pursuing that, for brevity, since my aim [here] is only the manifest, evident commandments. With all that we have recounted of them of these statements, they claim that they transmit, that they took from prophecy, that they are the people of the language, and that they are the [true] reasoners and doers. I shall later recount their claim in this and take up all that they claim for it — with its corruption. I now mention in the following bab some of their statements concerning the other commandments, of what amounts to abandoning the religion utterly and requires unbelief (kufr) and irreligion (ilḥād) — for in this too is an alerting to their case, and a refutation of what they claim of having transmitted from prophecy. ---

4.title_en: Some of Their Statements Concerning Matters Other Than the Commandments, of What Amounts to Unbelief and Irreligion

segments.en: We have already recounted of them, at the beginning of the preceding bab, their statements on corporealization and likeness, and what they reported in the "Shiʿur Qomah" of [God's] measures and limits — from the toes of the feet to the head. They said, at the end of the matter, that every day Michael binds the phylacteries upon His [the Creator's] head, and that from the sole of His foot to the limit of His stature is two hundred thirty-six thousand parasangs — contrary to the saying of Scripture [Job 11:7]: "הַחֵקֶר אֱלוֹהַּ תִּמְצָא? אִם עַד תַּכְלִית שַׁדַּי תִּמְצָא?" and His saying [Isa 40:18]: "וְאֶל מִי תְּדַמְּיוּן אֵל וּמַה דְּמוּת תַּעַרְכוּ לוֹ."

They said in the "Otiyyot de-Rabbi ʿAqiva" that the Creator — exalted and exalted — said: "I took Enoch son of Jared, and raised the head of his stature above you among all the tall of stature, and made his throne greater than My throne, and his glory greater than My glory." In those same "letters" they also said that the Creator — exalted — bound His hands with the hands of the righteous when He calls them in the Garden of Eden, and will say to them: "I have come to you only to eat and drink with you."

They said in the book ascribed to "Ishmael" — which is the "Book of Meṭaṭron" — that Meṭaṭron binds the phylacteries each morning upon the head of the Creator — far exalted is our God above this! — and that every day, when the time comes for reciting the [chapter of] the Unification in the morning, Meṭaṭron stands in awe, trembling, and dread, and binds the phylacteries upon the head of the Creator; and that the height of Meṭaṭron's stature is the height of the seven heavens and the seven seas, and the height of the heights of the [angels]. And the Creator — magnified and exalted — sits upon His throne, and he [Meṭaṭron] stands on his feet and cannot bind the phylacteries until he stretches and raises his leg.

They have mentioned in the Talmud that the Creator — exalted — prays; and they grounded this on His saying [Isa 56:7]: "וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי" — and that His prayer is that He says [B. Berakhot 7a]: "יְהִי רָצוֹן מִלְּפָנַי שֶׁיִּכְבְּשׁוּ רַחֲמַי אֶת כַּעֲסִי… וְאֶתְנַהֵג עִם בָּנַי בְּמִדַּת רַחֲמִים." Blessed is He to whom belong [all] prayers and praises; far exalted and far raised is our God and Creator above what the extreme defilers ascribe to Him.

They said in the "Chapters of the Fathers" that you have no reward for reading and studying Scripture except in the company of the Rabbanites, and followed this by saying [B. Bava Metsiʿa 33a]: "אֵלּוּ שֶׁעוֹסְקִין בַּמִּקְרָא — מִדָּה וְאֵינָהּ מִדָּה. בַּמִּשְׁנָה — מִדָּה וְנוֹטְלִין עָלֶיהָ שָׂכָר. בַּגְּמָרָא — אֵין לְךָ מִדָּה גְּדוֹלָה מִזּוֹ. וּלְעוֹלָם הֱוֵי רָץ לַמִּשְׁנָה יוֹתֵר מִן הַמִּקְרָא." This contradicts the saying of Scripture [Josh 1:8]: "וְהָגִיתָ בּוֹ יוֹמָם וָלָיְלָה."

Scripture reported that, at the time of the Temple's destruction, mourning, weeping, and the like are obligatory on account of the transgressions, in His saying [Isa 22:11]: "וְלֹא הִבַּטְתֶּם אֶל יֹצְרָהּ" — closing [22:12]: "וַיִּקְרָא ה' צְבָאוֹת בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא לִבְכִי וּלְמִסְפֵּד." Yet they claimed, in "Tractate Ḥagigah" and in the "Answer of Ahab," that the weeping, the mourning, the sackcloth, and the ashes the Creator performed Himself. Does one who describes Him with weeping, mourning, and the wearing of sackcloth truly know God?

They said in the Talmud that God has a place called "the hidden places," in which He wept, per His saying [Jer 13:17]: "בְּמִסְתָּרִים תִּבְכֶּה נַפְשִׁי," and they said there that He says: "Woe to Me, that My house is destroyed and My children are exiled." They claimed that the angels surround Him, and that since His house was destroyed His stature is bent; and they said that He tears His hair with His hands, and that until now His judgment is not sealed. All this is contrary to the saying of Scripture [Job 26:14]: "וּמַה שֵּׁמֶץ דָּבָר נִשְׁמַע בּוֹ."

They said in the Talmud that when the Children of Israel grew slack in the Torah, the Creator became poor; they mean by it the Creator — exalted — by way of metaphor, lest a man ascribe the illness to His son. They grounded this on His saying [Eccl 10:18]: "בַּעֲצַלְתַּיִם יִמַּךְ הַמְּקָרֶה" — saying: the "roofing" (ha-meqareh) means only God, per [Ps 104:3]: "הַמְקָרֶה בַמַּיִם עֲלִיּוֹתָיו."

They said in their "Aggadah" known in the "Talmud of the school of Rabbi" that the Creator — exalted — learned from Moses three things. The first: from the story of the calf; when He wished to destroy the Children of Israel, saying [Exod 32:10]: "וְעַתָּה הַנִּיחָה לִּי וְיִחַר אַפִּי בָהֶם וַאֲכַלֵּם," Moses said to Him [Num 14:13]: "וְשָׁמְעוּ מִצְרַיִם כִּי הֶעֱלִיתָ בְכֹחֲךָ אֶת הָעָם הַזֶּה מִקִּרְבּוֹ," and [14:16]: "מִבִּלְתִּי יְכֹלֶת ה'" — and the Creator took notice [and refrained]. He said to the Creator: "You have given me life by Your word!"; and grounded it on His saying [Num 14:18]: "ה' אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב חֶסֶד." The second: that the Creator told Moses, in the story of Sihon, "וְהִתְגָּר בּוֹ מִלְחָמָה" [Deut 2:24] — yet Moses set this aside and did the opposite, in his saying [Deut 2:26]: "וָאֶשְׁלַח מַלְאָכִים מִמִּדְבַּר קְדֵמוֹת אֶל סִיחוֹן" with words of peace; and what he did was, with the Creator, the right thing. He said to him: "O Moses, I will annul My word and confirm yours!" — and accepted it from him, and used it thereafter, in His saying [Deut 20:10]: "כִּי תִקְרַב אֶל עִיר לְהִלָּחֵם עָלֶיהָ וְקָרָאתָ אֵלֶיהָ לְשָׁלוֹם." How far is anything more [a mark] of ignorance and feebleness than this, which they have ascribed to the [supposedly] All-Wise, of whom it is said [Dan 2:21]: "יָהֵב חָכְמְתָא לְחַכִּימִין וּמַנְדְּעָא לְיָדְעֵי בִינָה," who is the Giver of power to every possessor of power, of whom it is said [Ps 27 — i.e. the verse "from the LORD a man's steps…"], [Ps 147:5]: "גָּדוֹל אֲדוֹנֵינוּ וְרַב כֹּחַ," [147:10]: "לֹא בִגְבוּרַת הַסּוּס יֶחְפָּץ"?

It would be beyond the power of the enumerator to count their statements of this kind; so we have confined ourselves to mentioning this small portion — by which their unbelief and irreligion are made clear, and the falsity of those who claim that they transmit from prophecy. Enough for you is what they reported in the Talmud concerning "Eliezer son of Hyrcanus": they said that a group of sages was disputing about which vessels become impure, until they reached the "Oven of Akhnai," made of separate pieces and rings, mounted one upon another, with a piece of clay between each two pieces and a gap between each piece — does this oven become impure or not? The rest of the sages judged it impure, and Eliezer did not. Every proof he brought, they did not accept from him. So he testified by signs. A first sign arose for him: the water that was flowing downward turned and flowed upward; they did not accept it. He testified by a second sign — that a carob tree uprooted itself and moved cubits from its place; they did not accept it. A third sign arose for him — that the walls of the study-house leaned; they did not accept it. When he saw this, he testified by a "bat qol" that came forth from heaven — and the meaning of this with them is the voice of the Creator — which said: "What have you with Eliezer, when the truth is with him?" And Joshua son of Hananiah arose and gestured toward heaven…

He said [Song 7:6]: "מֶלֶךְ אָסוּר בָּרְהָטִים." And Eliezer already declared this in a "hymn" they pray on the Day of Atonement, "לְךָ הָאָרֶץ וְשׁוֹכְנֶיהָ," saying: "יַד ה' מְכֻוָּלָה." Perhaps this is what he [Muḥammad] said [Qurʾān 5, sūrat al-Māʾida 64]: "wa-qālat al-yahūd yad allāh maghlūla" — this fell to him and he took his saying from it.

What is more astonishing than their saying in the Talmud [B. Ḥagigah 16a]: "אִם רוֹאֶה אָדָם שֶׁיִּצְרוֹ מִתְגַּבֵּר עָלָיו, יֵלֵךְ לְמָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין מַכִּירִין אוֹתוֹ, וְיִלְבַּשׁ שְׁחוֹרִים וְיִתְעַטֵּף שְׁחוֹרִים, וְיַעֲשֶׂה מַה שֶּׁלִּבּוֹ חָפֵץ, וְאַל יְחַלֵּל שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא." By this saying they permitted lewdness and licentiousness — if a man wore black garments and went off to a place where he is unknown.

They said in the Talmud that Meṭaṭron is a lesser god, whose name is "Kem Anadu," and that before him is an altar, and the souls of the righteous offer upon it, and the souls of the masters of the Talmud sit around him, and the angels stand erect before him, and he studies Talmud and halakha with them. They did not cease studying until they dissented over the words of Scripture [Lev 13:4]: "וְאִם בַּהֶרֶת לְבָנָה הִיא" — they said: it is pure; and the Creator said: it is impure. Those souls around him did not accept it from Him. He sent an angel to take the soul of "Rabbah son of Naḥmani," for this Rabbah was a learned man, an expert; and the angel could not take his spirit, for he heard him studying Talmud. He returned to the One who sent him and told Him the tale. The Sender said to him: "Stand over him like the knife, and set upon him a storm-wind; when he is silent, take his spirit." He did so, and his soul went up saying: "Pure, pure!" — praises to the Creator, exalted — siding with His judgment. The Creator — exalted — said: "They have defeated Me!" This resembles the story we told of Eliezer son of Hyrcanus, and the Creator's saying: "My children have defeated Me!" In it is of [the same] good and abundance as in this and more. They said: out of honor for the soul of this "son of Naḥmani," his body was not given to the dogs. A scrap of a scroll was cast down from heaven to the academy of the people of Sura, written in it: that "Rabbah son of Naḥmani" had been summoned to guide the people of the Upper Academy. They arose and walked among the "marshes," the wildernesses, and the waters until they saw the birds and the vermin upon his corpse, and bore it and passed with it, and mourned three days. When they wished to part, another scrap fell from the cloud, written in it: "Whoever parts shall be among those put to death." So they returned to the gathering for seven days. Then a third scrap fell, [written in it]: "Return in peace." They left it and went. A storm-wind arose to destroy the world, for it wished to raise him up to heaven. One who asked — a man of the Arabs — said: "What is this?" They said to him: "'Son of Naḥmani' has been raised to heaven." Then he disputed with the Creator and said to Him: "You created 'son of Naḥmani,' and You took his spirit. Why ever do You destroy?" Then the wind was stilled. At the beginning of this story — a story that Rabbah son of Naḥmani gave the Creator the lie, annulled His statement, and the Creator confessed His being defeated by him, and that "son of Naḥmani's" statement is the truth and His statement — that is, the Creator's — is the contrary. And at the end of the story — that the Arab gave the Creator pause, alerted Him that He wished to do what is not right, and that the Creator turned back from what He wished to do.
They said that the Creator mourned for Methuselah seven days, per [Gen 7:10]: "וַיְהִי לְשִׁבְעַת הַיָּמִים וּמֵי הַמַּבּוּל."

They said that a man asked "Rav Abbahu," saying to him: "Is your God a priest?! — for He said [Exod 25:2]: 'וְיִקְחוּ לִי תְּרוּמָה.' If so, how, when He buried Moses — did He wash or immerse? If you say He washed in water — did He not say [Isa 40:12]: 'מִי מָדַד בְּשָׁעֳלוֹ מַיִם'? — for the water cannot contain Him or immerse Him." Rav Abbahu said: "He immersed in fire," and grounded it on His saying [Isa 66:15]: "כִּי הִנֵּה ה' בָּאֵשׁ יָבוֹא." He said: "And this is from the Torah, per His saying [Num 31:23]: 'כָּל דָּבָר אֲשֶׁר יָבֹא בָאֵשׁ תַּעֲבִירוּ בָאֵשׁ וְטָהֵר.'"

Thereafter they outdid the Christians in the very [matter of] contention and obstinacy; for the principles of the Christians in most of their statements rest on contention and obstinacy, since they used to acknowledge and recognize the truth of the legislation of the Jewish religion, and [then] abandoned it. When it was made clear to them, in what was translated for them of our books, that alteration and exchange had already befallen it — they took up the effrontery to claim that the Greek language is the ancient tongue; this is reported of "Kūfarī" and his like. Many of them claim that no alteration or exchange befell the translation — saying that Ptolemy the king gathered seventy elders of the Jews, separated them, set each two of them in [their own] place, and commanded them to translate the twenty-four books. They did so. The translations were collated — no difference was found among them. This is what they call "the Production of the Seventy." As for the Rabbanites, they affirm this statement of theirs, and call the king who did this "Talmiyos" (Ptolemy). Only they claim that the Creator — exalted and exalted — taught them all to write one [and the same] thing; and that they [the Seventy] altered ten things from what is in Scripture, writing them contrary to what they are. These are the things they claim the Seventy altered: [Gen 1:1] "בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים בְּרֵאשִׁית" (for "בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים"); [1:26] "אֶעֱשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצֶלֶם וּדְמוּת" (for "נַעֲשֶׂה"); [1:27] "זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בְּרָאוֹ" (for "בְּרָאָם"); [2:2] "וַיְכַל אֱלֹהִים בַּיּוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי וַיִּשְׁבֹּת בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי" (for "הַשְּׁבִיעִי"); [Gen 49:6] "וּבִרְצֹנָם עִקְּרוּ אֵבוּס" (for "שׁוֹר"); [Exod 4:20] "וַיִּקַּח מֹשֶׁה אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ וְאֶת בָּנָיו וַיַּרְכִּבֵם עַל נוֹשֵׂא אֲנָשִׁים" (for "הַחֲמֹר"); [Num 16:15] "חֹמֶד אֶחָד מֵהֶם" (for "חֲמוֹר"); [Lev 11:6 / Deut 14:7] "הָאַרְנֶבֶת קְצַרַת הָרַגְלַיִם" (for "אַרְנֶבֶת"); [Exod 12:40] "וּמוֹשַׁב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר יָשְׁבוּ בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם וּבְכָל הָאֲרָצוֹת" (for [Egypt] alone); [Deut 4:19] "אֲשֶׁר חָלַק ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֹתָם לְהָאִיר לְכָל הָעַמִּים" (for "לְכֹל הָעַמִּים"). By this saying they ascribed to the Creator — exalted — distortion and the teaching of falsehood; and this is the utmost of corruption, for one who teaches falsehood and dictates it has [thereby] done falsehood, and one who did falsehood has lied. This is one of the things charged against the "Ḥabariyya" (the extremists). [And the rejoinder: if the Creator altered the direction of these things, gathered by the Seventy, because they affect anthropomorphism — then He would have been obliged to alter the other verses too in which there are limbs: hand, eye, ear, mouth, and indeed the first verse of Genesis "אֲשֶׁר בָּרָא"; and ought He not to have altered [Exod 33:11]: "פָּנִים אֶל פָּנִים" which suggests speaking face to face? And so on; what is in Scripture of this kind the enumerator could not count. So their falsehood is exposed: for those very things they claimed were altered and exchanged are found among the Christians exactly as they are found with us, without alteration. The proof of this is that the Christians argue against us, to establish their statement of corporealization, by the saying of Scripture (Gen 1:26): "בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ."] And the opening of the Torah with them [the Aramaic Targum of Gen 1:1] is "בְּקַדְמִין בְּרָא אֱלָהָא." With this — there is enough in recounting all that has been said of them. Is there [need] to end with this very [matter]?

This is what has been exposed of [my] taking from their statements. Among them is one who, if any of this is mentioned before him, says: "This is a scandal!" Among them are those who claim that not all the Rabbanites say this, but only the rare one among them. It has even reached me that some of them say these things are not the Rabbanites' statement, but that the dissenters composed them and slipped them into the statements of the Rabbanites. So know this: if they take you up this way and pour [this] upon you, make use of curses against whoever said this and whoever knows that the Rabbanites said it and yet denies and multiplies [denials] — that you may suppress them by it. It had been my wish to argue in several things I have recounted of their statements — of what does not enter into the discussion of the commandments, such as their statement on corporealization, and that this Torah is not the Torah that Moses brought, and the like — and to refute what they claim of [received] tradition and transmission; but I have deferred this until I finish recounting what each sect held as distinctive, so that the response to them and to others may come one after another.

They have magnified the matter of the "Targum of Onqelos" of the Torah, and magnified it greatly, to the point that they claimed that Onqelos the proselyte uttered it from his mouth ("jāʾi, wa-rūyā, wa-malāʾi"), and joined it to the Torah of God, reading it with [the Torah] verse by verse. In it are wonders beyond measure; of this — his saying at [Gen 49:11] "אֹסְרִי לַגֶּפֶן עִירֹה," which he rendered "in his town" (his city); and the rendering of [Deut 23:18] "לֹא תִהְיֶה קְדֵשָׁה" — that he meant a daughter of Israel should not be married to a [male] slave, nor a son of Israel to a bondwoman; and he rendered [Exod 12:48] "וְכָל עָרֵל לֹא יֹאכַל בּוֹ" — that every apostate from Judaism shall not eat of it; and he rendered [Gen 28:21] "וְהָיָה ה' לִי לֵאלֹהִים" — "and the word of the LORD shall be God to me." With this — he dissented from the Rabbanites in several things. Of this — his saying that Enoch died, while they generally say he ascended to heaven alive; and his saying that the yemamah is "shafninim," while they know it is a rooster. ---

5.title_en: The Doctrine of the Samaritans, Which Dissents from That of the Whole Nation

segments.en: The Samaritans do not acknowledge any prophet other than "Moses" and "Joshua," and do not believe in anything of the books of prophecy except the Torah and the book of "Joshua." They do not recognize the Temple, and their prayer is toward Shechem. To this day they offer the sacrifices, and they have a priest who does not mix with them and does not take wives from among them — so far as has reached us. They do not mix with others nor draw near to anyone; and if one not of them drew near them, they washed themselves of him.

It is reported of them that they take the heads of the months by an intercalation of their own, which they call the intercalation of "Jeroboam." It is also reported of them that if a garment became impure for them, they put it in a jar-like vessel or the like, stopped up the vessel's mouth, and put it into water — and the garment, with them, was thereby purified without touching the water; for in this they took the saying of Scripture [Lev 11:32]: "וּבָא בַמַּיִם."
They are two groups: one of them called "Kūshān," the other "Dustān." One of the two groups does not acknowledge the maʿād (the world to come).

They have altered things in the reading of the Torah — of this, that they read [Exod 20:18]: "וְכָל הָעָם שׁוֹמְעִים אֶת הַקֹּלֹת" (for "רֹאִים"); and that they read [Gen 4:8]: "וַיֹּאמֶר קַיִן אֶל הֶבֶל אָחִיו: קוּם נֵצֵא הַשָּׂדֶה" (an addition to the Masoretic text); and other things, some of which will appear in our account of the doctrine of "Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī."

6.title_en: The Doctrine of the Sadducees, Which Is of This Kind

segments.en: Of this: they forbade the divorce explicitly permitted [in Scripture]. They also made all the months thirty days each — perhaps relying in this on the story of Noah.

They also removed the day of the Sabbath from the count of the days of the Passover festival, making them seven exclusive of the Sabbath; and likewise the Festival of Booths. Perhaps an analogy led them to this, and they made it obligatory from the saying of Scripture [1 Kgs 8:66]: "וּבַיּוֹם הַשְּׁמִינִי שִׁלַּח אֶת הָעָם," and His saying in another place [2 Chr 7:10]: "וּבְיוֹם עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה לַחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִי שִׁלַּח אֶת הָעָם" — for the "eighth" is the twenty-second day, and if they remove the Sabbath from the count of the eight, the "eighth" becomes the twenty-third day. "David son of Marwān al-Muqammiṣ" already reported something of their doctrine, which I shall mention at the end of the following bab.

The Maghāriyya take the heads of the months when the new moon appears to the eye. They have in this an argument that I shall mention when we come to treat the New Moon and its signs. It is reported of them that there were among them men who would not permit laughter. They have, on [certain] places of Scripture, far-fetched interpretations resembling idle tales.

"David son of Marwān" reported, in some of his books, of the Sadducees that they used to corporealize the Creator — exalted be His praise — taking up their statement on those descriptions which Scripture used of Him, of the descriptions that, in their plain sense, require corporealization. But of the Maghāriyya he reported the contrary of this — that they did not hold corporealization. Yet they too did not take those descriptions out of their plain sense, but claim that they are descriptions of one of the angels — the one who created the world. This is as will appear from the doctrine of "Benjamin al-Nahāwandī."
As for "Boethus" — who, we said, was the companion of "Zadok" — he used to say that the Festival of Weeks is only on the first day [of the week], as our own people [the Karaites] say.

8.title_en: Jesus, the Doctrine of the Christians, and What David al-Muqammiṣ Reported of the Origin of Their Religion

segments.en: The Jews are much divided concerning "Jesus": some of them claim that he laid claim to prophethood, and some denied this. As for the Rabbanites — they reported in the Talmud that they conceded his miracles, but claimed the miracles were worked for him by "sorcery" and "the hidden Name." As for "Benjamin" [al-Nahāwandī], it was reported to me of him that he claims five men of the Jews laid claim to prophethood, one of them Jesus; he said: of them Scripture says [Dan 11:14]: "וּבְנֵי פָּרִיצֵי עַמְּךָ יִנַּשְּׂאוּ לְהַעֲמִיד חָזוֹן וְנִכְשָׁלוּ." As for some of the Karaites — they claim that "Jesus" was a righteous man, and that his case was like the case of "Zadok," "ʿAnan," and others; the Rabbanites set themselves to kill him until they killed him, just as they sought to kill "ʿAnan" too, only that they were not able. This is their way with everyone who wished to dissent from them. And Jesus forbade divorce, as the Sadducees forbade it.

As for the religion of the Christians that they are upon now — "Paul" is the one who innovated it and brought it forth. He it is who ascribed divinity to "Jesus," and laid claim for himself to prophethood from "Jesus" his master. He brought no obligation at all and imposed nothing upon anyone, claiming that the religion is humility alone. They claim that fasting and prayer with them are not an obligation but voluntary; and he forbade nothing of foods, but permitted every animal — from the fly to the elephant.

As for the religion of the Christians that they are upon now — it is standing irreligion. That is: they claim that the Creator is one substance with three hypostases (aqānīm), and that He is one [that is] three and three [that is] one. For He is, with them, living and knowing; so "living" and "knowing" are two attributes of an essence: the essence is one hypostasis, and the two attributes are two hypostases — so by this they become three hypostases. They claim that the Messiah of whom the prophets gave glad tidings and whose coming was promised is "Jesus," and that he is one of the three hypostases. The three hypostases are: Son, Father, and Spirit. The Son is "Jesus," and he is divine-human; for the Creator — who is the essence — was united with him. This is the substance of their statements; they have differences in the details. They say that the House of which the prophets gave glad tidings that it would be built thereafter, and which "Ezekiel" beheld, is none other than what Zerubbabel built; and likewise all the glad tidings of which the prophets gave tidings have already passed and come to be.

As for the "moderns" (the [latter-day] philosophers) of the Christians — they claim that the obligations of the Torah were imposed on the Children of Israel only by way of punishment, and that they themselves chose them because they resemble the obligations of the Ṣābians (the Ṣābiʾa); this was only because they had been constrained to the doctrines of the Egyptians when they grew up among them, which are of the kind of the doctrines of the Ṣābians. They claim that the statement that "the Creator — exalted — is one substance in three hypostases" is a secret that God did not disclose to anyone of the ancients, since the minds of men then could not contain it; until Jesus came, and men arose who could contain it in their minds, so He disclosed it to them and made it known to them.
