They claim that the Creator's speech is co-eternal with Him — one of the things they rely on in argument; for "John" says at the opening of his Gospel — one of the four Gospels [John 1:1]: "בְּרֵאשִׁית הָיָה הַדָּבָר וְהַדָּבָר הָיָה אֵצֶל הָאֱלֹהִים וֵאלֹהִים הָיָה הַדָּבָר." With this, they hang upon things from our books, which I shall mention later, after I have concluded against them and stated what is against them from the side of the intelligible.

This is what "David son of Marwān al-Raqqī" reported of the origin of the religion of the Christians: "David son of Marwān al-Raqqī" — known as "al-Muqammiṣ" — was a philosopher; he was at first a Jew, and then converted to Christianity at Nisibis at the hands of a man called "Nānā." This "Nānā" was great among the Christians, for he was a complete philosopher whose craft was medicine. "David al-Muqammiṣ" studied with him for many years, mastered the principles and secrets of Christianity, and excelled in philosophy. He composed against the Christians two books in which he argued — both books well known. He also translated, from the books of the Christians and their commentaries, a commentary on Genesis, which he called "the Book of Creation," and a commentary on Ecclesiastes. "David son of Marwān" also said: The Christians — when they did not find in the Gospel decisive rulings on some matter — claimed that "Paul" and "Peter," who is "Abū Shāwul," the Jewish fisherman, established for them limits and rulings not in the Gospel or in the Torah — except the Sabbath. These two men commanded their observance, and said that these rulings are rulings the Messiah handed to them, and decreed and ruled by them. And when these rulings that "Paul" and "Peter" established did not supply what was needed, bishops gathered in the city of "Nicaea," and established for them rulings the former had not transmitted; these became authoritative and accepted — though they have for them no text in the Torah, the Gospel, or the canon of "Peter" and "Paul." Yet with them they are God's rulings, by which they decide, though there is no decision in [Scripture]; he said: whoever examines this knows it. Nor were it only these three hundred and eighteen bishops who established this for them; others established [rulings] for them too. He said: the cause of this is that their Gospel constrained them to believe the statement of every possessor of an opinion, with no argument from the Gospel.
The mention of the Trinity and incarnation — namely, that they said: […]

[Jesus said, Matt 5:17]: "I have not come to abolish [the Torah and the Prophets] but to fulfill. And whoever annuls one commandment of them shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven." As for the four Gospels: they are the Gospel of "Matthew," of "Mark," of "Luke," and of "John." As for "Matthew," he was a man of the toll-house (a tax-collector); "Mark" was a fisherman who caught fish from the lake of Tiberias; "Luke" was a disciple of "Paul" — who is "Abū Shāwul" — and was a physician; and "Paul" was a leather-worker. As for "John," he came after Jesus, and was of the kin of the one who had charge of Jesus in what he had charge of. He [al-Muqammiṣ] said: this Gospel is a book in which these [four] relate the story of "Jesus" from its beginning to its end: his coming, from whom he was born, and his genealogy. These four Gospels agree in [some] things and disagree in [others]. They disagree in the genealogy: for "Matthew" reckoned forefathers other than the forefathers "Luke" reckoned, while "Mark" mentioned no forefathers and no genealogy, and likewise "John." [Matthew traced the ascent upward — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron — down to David; Luke, [tracing] a natural genealogy down to David, then departs from the line "Matthew" reckoned by passing from "Solomon" to "Nathan" son of David; and the genealogy each gives is the genealogy of Joseph, the betrothed of "the mother of Jesus."] So there are here three difficulties: the first — two differing genealogies of Jesus; the second — that both are genealogies of Joseph, not of Jesus; the third — that if "the mother of Jesus" had no husband Joseph, then their genealogies do not fit: for they claim that Mary the mother of Jesus "was betrothed" to Joseph and that Joseph did not come in to her, but found her pregnant — so the statement of "Matthew" and "Luke" [makes the conception] "from the Holy Spirit." No mention of "Heli," "Jacob," and "Matthat" is found in the twenty-four books, nor in the historians of the Jews — neither in general nor [as] known in any genealogy. So the Christians contrived, and said that "Heli" is a man of theirs, "son of Nathan" born of David, and was the brother of "Jacob son of Nathan" born of "Solomon," his maternal brother; that the man "Heli" died childless, so "Jacob" his maternal brother came in to his wife and raised up seed for him — and "Joseph" was born. So Joseph was the son of the two men: of "Jacob" by nature, and of "Heli" by the imputation that is the raising up of seed. This is the statement of "David son of Marwān al-Muqammiṣ," which I have reported as it is, to show by it the unsoundness and weakness of the Christians' case. With this — the matter is too plain and clear to need elaboration. ---

What is clear is what we have already recounted of their use of vessels of gourd. We do not know what their reason in this is, except by way of conjecture and analogy from what has been reported of them. It may be that they agree with the Samaritans in keeping apart from the impurity [contracted] from any of the people; and perhaps too they hold that one who has drawn near a corpse in this age has no purification, since there is no purifying water; and that all the vessels taken from people's hands are impure, so they take vessels of gourd and make them for themselves.

What strengthens this conjecture: one of the reporters reported of them that no other person tells them anything of the reading [of the months?] and the harvest. This too is mysterious, and we do not know what its cause is.

It is also reported of them that they observe Sunday together with the Sabbath. This indicates that they incline to something of the doctrine of the Christians. This is what has reached me of their doctrine, some of which I saw in a book of one of the reporters in the account of the sects.

I had thought that the Qurʿiyya arose after "Jesus" and after Christianity, until I examined a book of "David son of Marwān al-Muqammiṣ" that he calls "Kitāb al-Ḍarāʿa," in which he mentions that the religion of Christianity was taken from the doctrine of the Sadducees and the Qurʿiyya together. This showed that the Qurʿiyya were before Christianity; so, [revising] what I had supposed, I have set their mention [where I did].

10.title_en: The Matters Disputed Between the Rabbanites of al-Shām and the Rabbanites of Iraq

segments.en: The matters in which they disagree would be some fifty, and we have no need to mention them all. We wish to mention of them the grave ones — those which oblige each group of them to ascribe to the other group, in the matter in which it dissented, the abandonment of the religion. For the dissension between the two groups in this matter is not less than what lies between the two groups together and the rest of the Karaites and the ʿAnanites. In this is the annulment of the "tradition" (qabbalah) they claim, and [of the claim] that their doctrines are taken from prophecy. Before we recount what they dispute among themselves, let us recount their statement on this matter. [They said:] that "Bayt Hillel" and "Bayt Shammai" dissented in [various] matters — some in which "Bayt Shammai" were lenient and "Bayt Hillel" stringent, and some in which "Bayt Hillel" were lenient and "Bayt Shammai" stringent. And the Rabbanites said: one who acted by what "Bayt Shammai" made stringent and by what "Bayt Hillel" made lenient would be a sinner; and likewise if he acted by what "Bayt Shammai" made lenient and "Bayt Hillel" stringent. The obligation [they held]: to act by one of the two statements, in its stringency and its leniency together. And one who inclined to one of the two parties altogether was approved. Had their scandal appeared in no [other] point than this, it would suffice to leap [at it]; for they made two contradictory statements both true, and held that whoever held to either of them was in the right.

Of the dissension between them: "Bayt Shammai" forbade killing a louse on the day of the Sabbath, and "Bayt Hillel" permitted it. Those who came later said: we hold the opinion of the school of "Bayt Hillel." They dissented over His saying [Exod 22:4]: "וּמֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם." Some of them said: this refers to the injured party, and so He said "the best of his field" — for he knows that fields and vineyards may contain thorns, brush, much vegetation of trees, reeds, and the like, but also good and precious fruits; so [the owner] is obliged, if he turned his beast loose and it grazed in that good field, to pay for what it grazed and ruined. So His saying "the best" refers to what preceded — the sense being "[the beast] grazed in the best of his field" — and His saying "shall pay" stands by itself. Others said: it refers to the doer [the one who pays].

Of what is between the people of al-Shām and the people of Iraq of dissension — the people of al-Shām make the bride-price (mohar) for a virgin two hundred zuz, and for a widow one hundred zuz; while the people of Iraq, the bride-price with them is twenty-five zuz. This requires that the marriage of the people of Iraq, with the people of al-Shām, is not a valid marriage — since they do not pay the obligatory bride-price. And if it is a valid marriage, and there is no fixed limit to the bride-price, what is the meaning of "two hundred zuz"? Yet they have said in the "Mishnah" a statement that contradicts the statement of all concerning the bride-price; namely [M. Qiddushin 1:1]: "הָאִישׁ מְקַדֵּשׁ בְּפָרוּטָה אוֹ בִּשְׁוֵה פְּרוּטָה." So if it is permitted for a man to betroth his wife with a single coin (fals), is it not annulled that there is here a limit — neither twenty-five, nor two hundred, neither more nor less?

Of this — that the people of Iraq, if a woman was nursing and her husband died, do not permit her to marry in less than two years; while the people of al-Shām permit her marriage at eighteen months. This requires that the child born to her, with the people of Iraq, is a "child of fornication" (mamzer); for she married upon the forbidden. We have already said before that the people of al-Shām examine by the finger, while with the people of Iraq this is close to lewdness. And of this: that the people of Iraq forbid the one who consummated [marriage] to return to intercourse except after seven days, while the people of al-Shām permit it. If a child came of that intercourse, it is, with the people of Iraq, a "child of fornication." Correspondingly, the people of al-Shām are obliged [to hold] that whoever was made pregnant from the night of consummation — that child must be a "child of fornication"; for consummation, with them, must be only by the finger.

Of this: the people of Iraq hold that one may set the pot in the oven before the entry of the Sabbath, so that it cooks on the Sabbath; while the people of al-Shām forbid this. So the people of Iraq, with the people of al-Shām, are Sabbath-profaners without doubt. And of this: the people of Iraq do not wash the hands [after contact with] one who died in their hands, nor [after] contact [with a corpse]; while the people of al-Shām wash the hands of this — even on the Day of Atonement, on which washing is forbidden. So the people of Iraq, with the people of al-Shām, are perpetually impure. One of the elders (shuyūkh) already told me that he saw in the evening people who do not wash the hands [after] contact. I mention this because, if they heard it, they would deny and contradict it — but the truth is sound. And of this: the people of al-Shām purify their hands with water, and the people of Iraq with stones. We have already said that the people of Iraq permit a menstruant to do all the work of the house — cooking, baking, and the rest — while the people of al-Shām forbid this. This is like the foregoing statements.

Of this: the people of Iraq permit, on the day of the Sabbath of the days of the Festival of Booths, [carrying] the myrtle, and forbid the taking of the palm-branch (lulav); while the people of al-Shām hold the contrary. And of this: the people of Iraq permit weighing the meat on the festival-day, while the people of al-Shām forbid putting it on the scales at all, even to guard it from the mouse. So the people of Iraq, with the people of al-Shām, are festival-profaners. And of this: the people of Iraq circumcise with water, the people of al-Shām with earth. So with each group of them, the circumcision of the other group is not a [valid] circumcision.

Of this: the people of Iraq examine the sheep (the permitted from the forbidden) by inspecting the lung, while the people of al-Shām do so by inspecting the head. An elder of the elders of "al-Raqqa" reported that he had been at the Temple, and that a ewe was inspected by the head and came out forbidden, but inspected by the lung came out permitted; and another ewe was the contrary. So each group of them, with the other group, eats ṭerefah. And of this: the people of Iraq do not hold the slaughter of an animal [valid] until it has been born eight days, while the people of al-Shām slaughter it from its [first] day. So the people of al-Shām, with the people of Iraq, perpetually eat the forbidden. And of this: the people of Iraq do not hold that a woman may be betrothed in the seventh year, while the people of al-Shām hold this. So whoever married in that year, with the people of al-Shām, is not validly married with the people of Iraq, and her children are not legitimate.

Of this: the people of Iraq hold that carrying coins is permitted on the Sabbath, while the people of al-Shām forbid even drawing near them. So the people of Iraq, with them, are Sabbath-profaners. And of this: the people of Iraq take the festival for two days, the people of al-Shām for one day. So the people of al-Shām, with the people of Iraq, are festival-profaners, falling under [Deut 13:1]: "וְלֹא תִגְרַע מִמֶּנּוּ"; and the people of Iraq, with the people of al-Shām, take a festival God did not make obligatory, falling under His saying [ibid.]: "לֹא תֹסֵף עָלָיו."

All that we have recounted of this — some we took [first-hand], some we learned [by report]. It is found and recorded in their books, and some of them already collected some of it in a separate book, from which we took and learned. So let not [the Rabbanites] busy your hearts with this, nor [should you] turn to it [as a charge against us]; for it is they upon whom the disgrace and the contradiction fell in this — from the very place where they claimed that all that is in their hands is transmitted from prophecy. What is of this kind may admit of no dissension at all; and in the falling of dissension [upon it] is a refutation of the statement of whoever claims this. As for us — we bring forth knowledge by deriving it with our intellects; and what is of this kind, we do not deny that dissension may fall upon it. We shall later recount what the "dissenters" claim in this, by way of reflection, and the answer to all of it. ---

11.title_en: The Doctrine of Abū ʿĪsā, Who Is ʿObadiah al-Iṣfahānī

segments.en: We have already reported that Abū ʿĪsā laid claim to prophethood, and that his miracle, with his adherents, was that he was an illiterate who could neither write nor read, yet brought forth books and scrolls — and that this can be only by prophethood. As for his doctrines and statements: he forbade the divorce explicitly permitted [in Scripture] — as the Sadducees and Christians forbade it — and made obligatory seven prayers each day, going in this to the saying of David [Ps 119:164]: "שֶׁבַע בַּיּוֹם הִלַּלְתִּיךָ עַל מִשְׁפְּטֵי צִדְקֶךָ." He forbade meat and [wine-]drinking — not from Scripture, but by claiming that God commanded him so by prophecy. He greatly strengthened and magnified the matter of the Rabbanites, until he placed them in something resembling the rank of the prophets, and claimed that God told him to pray with the Eighteen [Benedictions] and with the recital of the Shemaʿ, as the Rabbanites say. He did this only to win over, by means of it, the hearts of the commonalty and the majority. For this reason the Rabbanites and the majority do not [much] reckon with the ʿĪsawiyya, and do not regard them with the eye with which they regard the ʿAnanites and the Karaites.

I once asked "Jacob ben Ephraim al-Shāmī," saying to him: "Why did you draw the ʿĪsawiyya near and intermarry with them — they being upon what you know, ascribing prophethood to one not fit for it?" He said: "Because they did not dissent from us in the festivals." So this indicates that the appearance of unbelief, with people, is easier [to bear] than the appearance of dissension in a festival that they have innovated. Abū ʿĪsā acknowledged the prophethood of "Jesus son of Mary" and the prophethood of the prophet of the Muslims, claiming that each of them was sent to his own people and commanded the reading of the Gospel and the Qurʾān and the knowledge of their interpretations; and he claimed that the Muslims and the Christians — each nation of them was bound by what is in their hands, as Judaism was bound by what is in theirs. What brought him to acknowledge the prophethood of these two persons was a safeguard for his case and a shield for his words and for what he claimed of prophecy; for had he given them the lie and not acknowledged them, men would have been quicker to deny him. So his affirming of the two was in the hope that in it would be the completion of his case; but what he hoped of this came to nothing, and his hope was cut off. We shall make clear the corruption of his claim and the falsity of his statement later. ---

12.title_en: The Doctrine of Yudghan, Who Is the Shepherd

segments.en: "Yudghan" too laid claim to prophethood, and his adherents claim that he is the Messiah, that he did not die, and they await his return. The Yudghanites forbid meat and [wine-]drinking, and make much use of prayer and fasting. They claim that the Sabbaths and the festivals lapse in this age, and are only a "remembrance" (dhikr). Some of the Karaites have already shared with them in this statement — we shall mention it later, together with the answer to them.

13.title_en: The Doctrines Distinctive to ʿAnan the Exilarch and Those Who Followed Him

segments.en: Of this: he permitted, on the Sabbath, light carrying, in his saying: "It is not permitted to you to carry except on the [shoulder-]frames" — relying on [Num 7:9]: "אֶלָּא בַּכָּתֵף יִשָּׂאוּ." This is manifestly [self-]undoing. As for [some] of his adherents — they claim that he meant by it carrying within the houses, so that people not be permitted to carry in their houses on their frames. But the plain sense of his words does not indicate what they say — we shall explain this in its place. He permitted prayer only in a defined place, which he calls "the qinyah." He claimed that whoever ate, during "the seven days of unleavened bread," unleavened bread of wheat, was as one who ate leaven. He made circumcision obligatory with scissors and nothing else, and commanded that the milah be done with a "ḥarṣa" — small and large — together with oil of walnut. Whoever departs from these things is, with him, uncircumcised; and likewise one circumcised by a man who does not act so is uncircumcised and must repeat his circumcision. He made the circumcision of an adult obligatory on the eleventh of the month, exclusive of the rest of the days of the month. If a woman wished to enter the religion, she enters on the eighth of the month.

He made the seeking of [the barley of] the new-barley (aviv) obligatory on the twenty-fourth of Shevaṭ, claiming that Shevaṭ is the month of intercalation, not Adar. By the plain sense of his statement, he would permit [marriage to] the paternal aunt and the maternal aunt who are not from the [same] father; his adherents flee from this in the utmost flight. He permitted a man to marry the daughter of his father's wife — if his father had no child by her, that is, by her mother; and he claimed that the saying of Scripture [Lev 18:18] "וְאִשָּׁה אֶל אֲחֹתָהּ" means a woman and her sister's daughter. He claimed that the saying of Scripture [Lev 15:8] "וְכִי יָרֹק הַזָּב בַּטָּהוֹר" — that the woman is excluded from it: if a man with a flux spat upon a pure woman, she did not become impure. He made obligatory a fast of seventy days: from the thirteenth of Nisan to the twenty-third of Sivan. He made obligatory the fast of the seventh day of each month, and made obligatory the fast of the day of Esther. He made intercourse obligatory by day, and made it obligatory that a man have intercourse by night and by day more than once. He made intercourse with a pregnant woman obligatory only after she has been [pregnant] three months.

If the fifteenth of Nisan fell on the Sabbath, he deferred the taking of the festival to Sunday, which is the sixteenth; and likewise for the Festival of Booths. He did not make obligatory the impurity [contracted] from water, and claimed that a [household] vessel does not become impure from a [household] vessel. He brought down the impurity [contracted] from the corpse in this age, and did not make obligatory the impurity from slaughter. He claimed that the mouse of "the two flanks": if it was slaughtered, its impurity was less than the impurity of a corpse. He claimed [a rule concerning] the dead, and that its ruling is the ruling of the menstruant. He made obligatory the impurity only upon one who drew near intentionally; and claimed that the mouse does not convey impurity until it dies on the ground; and claimed that the impure, if he does not immerse from a [household] vessel, is not purified. He permitted the menstruant to stand in the "camp," and permitted the menstruant to discharge [her impurity] in a hollow with earth beneath. He did not permit [the company of] the pure and holy in the religion to one who dissented from him in [even] a single obligation. He made some impurity obligatory only upon one twenty years old, and some upon one five years old. He claimed that the young of a pure beast — if it died before eight days had passed for it — does not convey impurity. It is reported of him that he held [the doctrine of] "transmigration" (tanāsukh), and that he composed a book on it. We have seen some of his adherents holding this opinion. We shall later recount the statement of those who held transmigration and the passing of souls, and the answer to them. ---

14.title_en: The Doctrines Distinctive to Benjamin al-Nahāwandī

segments.en: He claimed that the Creator — exalted — created only one angel, and that this angel is the one who created the whole world, who sent the prophets, dispatched the messengers, established the miracles, and commanded and forbade; and he it is who originates whatever comes to be in the world — not the first Creator. He claimed that the levirate (yibbum) is obligatory only upon the king. He claimed that the saying of Scripture [Deut 21:15] "וְהָיָה הַבֵּן הַבְּכוֹר לַשְּׂנִיאָה" requires that the beloved [wife], even if she preceded in bearing, her son is not the firstborn; rather the firstborn is according to the unloved [wife], whether earlier or later — after both are firstborn. He claimed that the saying of Scripture [Exod 22:1] "אִם בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת יִמָּצֵא הַגַּנָּב וְהֻכָּה וָמֵת" was meant for any breach whatever — even an old breach that he did not dig himself and [made] not by demolition. He claimed that the saying of Scripture [Deut 23:16] "לֹא תַסְגִּיר עֶבֶד אֶל אֲדֹנָיו" [means]: if he was the slave of one of the Children of Israel and fled from him to you, it is not permitted for you to return him to him. He forbade marriage to a nursing woman, and made the obligations binding upon a minor from the time he speaks.

He used to permit the taking of the heads of the months by the [calculated] number — except Nisan and Tishrei: these he permitted to be taken only by the sighting of the new moon. He also held that the slaughter of a bird [requires] cutting (dhabḥ) and severing the neck (meliqah) together. He claimed that the consecrated [woman], if a man forced her in the wilderness even with her consent, is not obliged to be put to death. He claimed that one who came forth from the womb dead does not convey impurity from it; rather the impurity is from one who died in the open air. He claimed that the grave which conveys impurity to one who draws near it is the grave that is outside; but the grave that is within a house does not convey impurity to one who draws near it. He claimed that the garments of a woman with a flux, in which she lay and which had become for her a riding-seat or a sitting-place — if a man drew near them while they were stripped off her, he becomes impure from them and must wash his clothes; but if he drew near them while they were worn, he need only wash the body. He claimed that the time of the aṣīl does not receive impurity — that is, it is a time in which a person does not become impure. ---

"Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī" abolished the "written and the read" (the ketiv and the qere), claiming that the reading must be according to what is written. Another statement is reported of him that contradicts this one — namely that he claimed there are in Scripture things not as they are now written. Such is his saying [Gen 4:8]: "וַיֹּאמֶר קַיִן אֶל הֶבֶל אָחִיו" — he claimed there was after it "קוּם נֵצֵא הַשָּׂדֶה"; and His saying [Exod 20:18]: "וְכָל הָעָם רֹאִים אֶת הַקֹּלֹת" — he claimed it was "שׁוֹמְעִים אֶת הַקֹּלֹת," since sounds are not seen but heard. We have already said that this belongs to the Samaritans; perhaps he heard it from their statement and took it from them. He said: His saying [Exod 16:35] "וּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אָכְלוּ אֶת הַמָּן" is only "יֹאכְלוּ"; for they, at the time of this statement, had not [yet] eaten it forty years, but [Scripture] reported that they would eat it forty years. Likewise His saying [Gen 46:15] "כָּל נֶפֶשׁ בָּנָיו וּבְנוֹתָיו שְׁלֹשִׁים וְשָׁלֹשׁ" — he claimed it was "שְׁלֹשִׁים וּשְׁתַּיִם," and that this is an error of the scribe.

With him: whenever the new moon is born — which is the time of its parting from the sun — that time is the head of the month, and from that time prayer and offering are obligatory, even if it is an hour before sunset. He permitted, on the day of the Sabbath, eating what the "dissenters" prepared on the Sabbath, such as cooked eggplant, fruits picked on the Sabbath, and the like. He has many statements of the utmost corruption, ugliness, and grotesquerie. With this, he sets out in his books the disparagement of "ʿAnan" and ascribes to him folly and foolishness. We have already reported above what he commanded his adherents to write upon his grave [2 Kgs 2:12]: "רֶכֶב יִשְׂרָאֵל וּפָרָשָׁיו." ---

16.title_en: Abū ʿImrān al-Tiflīsī and Mālik al-Ramlī

segments.en: We have already said that neither of these two composed a book on the commandments, but dissented from the majority in small matters, such as: [keeping] the Festival of Weeks on the first day [of the week], the prohibition of the fat-tail (alyah) and the rump-fat (ʿaqavah), [the prohibition of] the brother's daughter and the sister's daughter, and the like.

As for "al-Tiflīsī" — he held [the calendar] by the parting [of the moon from the sun], following the statement of "Ismaʿīl"; except that he dissented from him in that he took the head of the month from the day on which the parting falls. He has answers to questions of [certain] people which he ascribes to "Ḥīwī," and he also has pages on the permitting of meat.

As for "Mālik al-Ramlī" — it is reported of him that he stood at the Temple and reported that the rooster used to be offered upon the altar that was in this House — meaning "the altar of the LORD." This is the act of an ignorant man.

This one too is one of the ignorant dissenters; namely, that he permitted [marriage and intercourse, the] "lawful pleasures of worldly things." It was [my view], and the view of others, that he it was who innovated this doctrine; but one of the elders of the ʿUkbarīs informed me that he took it from some of the people of the mountains, and that it is no unbelief, for innovations are many among the people of the mountains — only that Mīshawayh brought it forth, publicized it, and argued for it.

Mīshawayh claimed that the Festival of Weeks must be on a Sunday, but he does not know which Sunday. This doctrine belongs also to a group of the Baṣrans, except that [their] reckoning was with the majority. He claimed that the Passover must always be on a Thursday, so that the Day of Atonement be on the Sabbath; for it is said of it [Lev 23:32]: "שַׁבַּת שַׁבָּתוֹן." The meaning, with him: two Sabbaths — one the Sabbath, the other the Day of Atonement. He was in doubt about the knowledge of the heads of the months — not knowing by what [criterion] they must be taken.
They reported that he used to say to his adherents: "All the [received] tradition (qabbalah) is easy. Hold to what is in your hands" — meaning the festival of the majority.

He claimed that on the Sabbath no offering may be brought at all, and that the saying of Scripture [Num 28:10] "עֹלַת שַׁבַּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ" means "for the Sabbath," and that it used to be offered before the Sabbath for the sake of the Sabbath.
He claimed that the prayer-direction (qibla), in every place, must be toward the west, and that whoever is in Egypt or the West turns toward the Temple when he prays.

18.title_en: The Doctrines Distinctive to Daniel al-Dāmaghānī

segments.en: First: his denial of reflection upon the intelligible (al-naẓar fī al-maʿqūl), and his censure of its practitioners. This is recorded in more than one place of his books. Also: that he does not affirm the angels in the way the Children of Israel affirm them — as living forms, knowing, present, [sent] on missions, in the manner in which the prophets were dispatched. Rather, he claimed that this name — I mean our saying "angel" and "angels" — applies only to the bodies through which God works His acts, such as fire, clouds, winds, and the like. Another statement is reported of him in this, which I shall mention elsewhere, and I shall mention the answer to him. Also: he forbids the blood of fish, and permits of the locust only the four kinds mentioned by their names. He forbade intercourse by night, lest the [morning] prayer escape a man. He made obligatory the impurity [contracted] from the earth in this age. It is reported of him that he used to say: the obligations are binding only upon one twenty years old. He forbade on the Sabbath [certain] things, such as washing the hand with ushnān (soapwort), and the like. He forbade the lamp on the festival eve — in the manner the majority do on the Sabbath eve. He claimed that the saying of Scripture [Lev 1:15] "וְהִקְרִיב הַכֹּהֵן… וּמָלַק אֶת רֹאשׁוֹ" is an act [performed] after the slaughter. It is reported of him that he used to permit the testimony of the Muslims regarding the sighting of the new moon.

These, then, are the substance of the statements of those who have appeared down to this age, so far as has reached us. Some of these sects have already lapsed — such as the Maghāriyya, the Sadducees, and likewise the adherents of "Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī," of whom no one remains; nor is there anyone who submits to reflection in this age who inclines to his statement. As for the ʿAnaniyya — they have dwindled greatly, until there came to them one who came in [their] diminishing. As for the adherents of "Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī" — what remains of them, in Damascus alone, is like twenty souls. As for the Yudghanites — there is of them a small remnant in Iṣfahān. But dissension has multiplied greatly in this age among our own people; and we shall set out the dissension that is among them in [matters of] principle — so that we may not leave anything that needs treatment unmentioned. ---

19.title_en: The Matters in Which the Karaites of This Generation, and Before, Dissent — Among Those Not Ascribed to Any of the Sects Already Mentioned

segments.en: Among them is one who forbids washing from impurity on the day of the Sabbath; one who does not hold that he may wash his face on the Sabbath; one who does not hold the setting out of the dish on the Sabbath, nor the spreading of the bed — if he wishes to eat food, he draws close to where the food is until he eats it. Among them is one who holds the setting out of the dish and the spreading of the bed [permissible] but does not hold their removal [permissible], since setting out the dish and spreading the bed are for the need of the Sabbath, while removing them has no need for the Sabbath. Among them is one who does not hold the wearing of the "takkah" (the drawing-up of the trousers) on the Sabbath. Among them is one who holds that he may do on the Sabbath what he will use after the Sabbath, of what is permitted to be done on the Sabbath for the Sabbath — such as cooling water and the like; this belongs to some of the Baghdadis. Among them is one who does not hold that food may be left in its heat until the entry of the Sabbath, but [holds that] he should cool it before the entry of the Sabbath, claiming that if it remains hot, there falls upon it on the Sabbath an act, an increase, and a diminution; this belongs to some of the Tustarīs. And among them is one who denies this and holds also the keeping of [food] hot in the oven to eat it on the Sabbath. Among them is one who does not permit cooking and baking on any of the festivals except the Passover alone, claiming that the permission applies to it and not to another. It has reached me that some Tustarīs have lately [arisen] who permit on the festival only what is permitted on the Sabbath, claiming that the saying of Scripture [Exod 12:16] "אַךְ אֲשֶׁר יֵאָכֵל לְכָל נֶפֶשׁ" resembles His saying [Exod 16:25] "אִכְלֻהוּ הַיּוֹם."

Among them is one who holds [the festival] by the moist new-barley; one who does not take the month of the new-barley until the standing-grain (jirf) is found in all the land of the Children of Israel; one who takes [it] if the reaping was completed in a single plot (qarāḥ); and one who does this by [mere] inclining [of the ear toward ripeness]. Among them is one who does not hold carrying-out [of objects] on the Sabbath; one who does not hold the carrying-out from the place in which he sits to another inhabited place either, even if there is between the two places no courtyard and no partition; and one who holds [it permissible]. Among them is one who holds the wearing of a ring on the Sabbath, and one who does not — and not on a festival either. Among them is one who permits the statement of "one [witness]" regarding the sighting of the new moon, and one who permits it only by two witnesses. Some of the Baghdadis used to take the new-barley by a place in Baghdad — claiming that he had [thereby] intercalated it, and that it stands for the Holy Land. Among them is one who, if he sought the moon on the twenty-ninth and did not see it, then saw it after that, took the head of the month on that day; and one who does not hold this. Among them is one who follows the Exilarch in the intercalation of the day in [both] the Passover and the Festival of Booths together; one who follows him in this for the Passover but not for the Festival of Booths. Among them is one who follows "ʿAnan" also in the prohibition of circumcision on the day of the Sabbath, though most of them permit it.

Among them is one who holds that if he did not eat unleavened bread on any of the seven days, he transgresses — after [the rule that] he must not eat leaven; and one who makes its eating obligatory every day. Among them is one who claims that the time of the aṣīl is the whole of the [present] day; one who claims it is the whole of the morrow; and one who claims it is of the [present] day and of the morrow — following what "ʿAnan" said. Among them is one who holds that once the sun has set the Sabbath has gone out; and one who does not bring it out until the light has faded. Among them is one who permits reading any script other than Hebrew on the day of the Sabbath; and one who does not permit this. Among them is one who permits eating the flesh of sheep and cattle in the exile; and one who does not. Among them is one who permits eating the fish that died in the hands of the dissenters; and one who does not. Among them is one who holds eating the scalded kid (gedi ḥalūṭ); and one who does not, claiming that the fat is cooked with it. Among them is one who holds eating the slaughter of the majority, and one who does not permit it. Among them is one who permits the saʿīr (rooster?), one who forbids it, and one who claimed he does not know whether it is permitted or forbidden.

Among them is one who holds [the rule of] "a single intermediary" in impurity, claiming that this is [the right view]; one who holds "several intermediaries"; and one who holds no intermediary at all. Among them is one who makes the midday prayer obligatory every day; and one who holds it only on a fast-day. Among them is one who claims that if the Passover fell on a Sabbath eve, it must be transferred to the second month. Among them is one who holds washing from impurity in hot water, and one who does not. Among them is one who holds washing from impurity only in fresh water (ʿadhb), and one who holds it only in living water. The ancient Karaites of the Baṣrans claimed that the Festival of Weeks is only [on] a Sunday, but did not know which Sunday; and among them were some who claimed that it lapses in this age; and among them, too, were some who claimed that all the festivals lapse in this age, being only a "remembrance." Some of the Syrian Karaites held that a man may fast from one thing and not another in the voluntary fast. Some of the Khurasanian Karaites forbid the "written and the read" (the qere and the ketiv), reading only what is written; and of these is one who does so with the Name (of glory), [reading] it as "Yāh Hāh," claiming that whoever reads it as "Adonai" has [thereby] disbelieved.

Among the Karaites of Khurasan and the mountains is one who claims that the promised Messiah has already come and gone, and that the House, too, is the one Zerubbabel built, none other remaining. Of these, too, is one who annuls the resurrection of the dead, claiming that what Scripture reported of this was meant [as] the revival of the nation from the exile and from abasement. Some of the Baghdadis claimed that Enoch and Elijah have already died, and that they may not have ascended to heaven in their bodies. Of the "innovators" among them are men of the Baṣrans and the Tustarīs who claimed that wearing the sandal and the belt without need is forbidden on the Sabbath; and likewise wearing more than one tunic, and the cloak (ridāʾ), and everything that need does not lead one to wear, such as the girdle (zunnār) and the like. Among them is one who holds extinguishing the fire on the Sabbath if he had set it to do so before the Sabbath — rather, he makes it obligatory. Likewise they make obligatory the stopping of the water that irrigates the sown field on the Sabbath, if he had set it to be stopped before the Sabbath; and likewise they close the mill on the day of the Sabbath, [for] some such [reason], so that it not grind on the Sabbath. The wonder is that they permit — indeed make obligatory — acts and motions on the Sabbath, and forbid abstention and rest.

They dissented over "doubtful cases" (shukūk), some making them obligatory and some not. They dissented over the contracting of the light impurity by the grave impurity: some held it obligatory, some not. They dissented over the impurity of a house from the corpse: some held it, some not. They dissented over one who let the fixed time of washing — which Scripture made obligatory — pass: some permitted him to wash at any time he wished, and some permitted it only at a comparable time. They dissented over the dwelling of strangers in the booth: some held it obligatory, some not.

These are what came to mind to record of their dissension; and the matter is increasing every day. It may be that one of our own people who reads this will blame his [own] memory for it — for there are among the Rabbanites those who reproach us with it, doing so under our reproaching of them with the dissension between the people of al-Shām and the people of Iraq. So let not [the Rabbanites] busy your hearts with this, nor turn to it. For it is they upon whom the disgrace and contradiction fell in this — only from the place where they claimed that all that is in their hands is transmitted from prophecy. What is of this kind may admit of no dissension at all; and in the falling of dissension is a refutation of the statement of whoever claims this. As for us — we bring forth knowledge by deriving it with our intellects; and what is of this kind, we do not deny that dissension may fall upon it. We shall later recount what the "dissenters" — of the obligation of reflection — claim from this angle, and the answer to it. May this discourse be brought to completion by the help of God and His power. Blessed be the Lord forever; Amen and Amen. ---
